How to read this guide

This guide explains QUIZZY from the top down. Sections 1 and 2 give you the big picture, section 3 defines every technical term and technology, sections 4 to 9 walk through the code in detail, sections 10 to 12 cover deployment, security and limitations, and sections 13 and 14 are for interview practice and for things to fix.

Everything here was written by reading the code as it exists now. When an older note (such as DECISIONS.md) or a code comment disagrees with the code, the code is treated as the truth and the difference is pointed out. File references are written as path → function, for example server/src/services/room.service.js → submitAnswer, so you can open the exact place in your editor.

Two small labels mark statements that could not be checked against the repository:

  • Inferred means the fact is deduced from how the code uses something (for example, a database table the code queries), because the SQL that created it is not in the repository.
  • Assumed means a hosting dashboard setting (Render or Vercel) that is not stored in the repository, described as the usual setup for this kind of project.

No secret values appear anywhere in this guide. Environment variables are referred to only by their names.

Technical terms are all defined in one place, section 3 ("Concepts and technologies"), grouped by topic. Everywhere else, a term with a dotted underline is a link to its definition, and an alphabetical index of terms with page numbers is at the very end.

In more detail: Each participant (browser, server, database) gets a vertical line, and each horizontal arrow is one message, in the order it happens; dashed arrows are replies. It is the clearest way to show "who talks to whom, and when", which is why section 9 uses one for every flow.

1.Overview

1.1 What QUIZZY does

QUIZZY is a live quiz app for classrooms, similar to Kahoot or Wayground (formerly Quizizz). A teacher, called the host, creates a multiple-choice quiz, either by typing the questions or by asking an AI to write them. In class, the host opens a room, which gets a 6-digit code and a QR code shown on the projector. Students join from their phones with just a nickname, answer the questions, and the host watches a live leaderboard update on the big screen. When the host ends the quiz, every student sees their final rank and the results are saved to the database.

Key terms here (defined in section 3): Real-time

1.2 Two kinds of users

Host (teacher)Student (player)
AccountNeeds an account (email + password, through Supabase Auth)No account. Only a nickname, typed when joining
DeviceLaptop connected to a projectorPhone, usually
Can doCreate quizzes (manually or with AI), open a room, start the quiz, end it, close the roomJoin a room, answer questions, see their own score and final rank
Screens/host, /host/new, /host/:quizId/ (enter code), /join/:code
Identified byTheir Supabase user ID (from a verified login token)Their socket ID (a random ID for one live connection)

1.3 Student-paced design

In Kahoot's classic mode everyone sees the same question at the same time, and the host clicks "next". QUIZZY works differently: it is student-paced. Once the host starts the quiz, every student gets question 1 and then moves on as soon as they answer. A fast student may be on question 8 while a slower one is on question 3. The host does not control the question flow at all; they only start and end the quiz.

This decision shapes the whole server design:

  • Each player has their own position in the quiz, stored as player.currentQuestionIndex.
  • When a student answers, the server sends only that student the result and their next question.
  • The leaderboard shows not just scores but also progress (questions answered out of total), so the host can see who is still working.
Real-life example

A teacher-paced quiz is like a class reading a book aloud together, one page at a time. A student-paced quiz is like a written exam: everyone gets the same paper, but each person turns the pages at their own speed, and the teacher can glance around to see who is on which page.

Key idea

QUIZZY stores quizzes permanently in a database (Supabase Postgres), but runs each live game in the server's memory. The live game is fast and temporary; only the final results are written back to the database at the end.

Where in the code
  • Per-player progress: server/src/services/room.service.js → addPlayer (creates currentQuestionIndex: 0) and → submitAnswer (advances it)
  • Sending each player their own question: server/src/sockets/socket.js, handlers for quiz:start and quiz:answer
  • Progress on the leaderboard: room.service.js → getLeaderboard (answered: player.currentQuestionIndex)
Interview tip

Open with one sentence: "QUIZZY is a student-paced live quiz app: hosts create quizzes, with AI if they like, and students join from their phones with a room code and answer at their own speed while the host watches a live leaderboard." Then say what makes it technically interesting: real-time WebSockets, server-side scoring so students can't cheat, and AI output that is validated before it reaches the user.

2.Architecture

2.1 The production system

QUIZZY is made of two programs and three external services:

  • The client (client/): a React app. Vite builds it into static files (HTML, JavaScript, CSS), and Vercel serves those files.
  • The server (server/): a Node.js program running Express (for normal web requests) and Socket.IO (for the live connection). Render runs it.
  • Supabase: the Postgres database (quizzes, questions, saved results) and the authentication service (host accounts and login tokens).
  • Google Gemini: the AI model that writes quiz questions.
Figure 2.1: Production architecture. Numbers show the usual order of connections.

Key terms here (defined in section 3): Client · Server · HTTPS and TLS · WebSocket · WSS (secure WebSocket) · CDN (Content Delivery Network)

2.2 What runs where

WhereWhat runs thereState it keeps
Browser (host or student)The React app: pages, components, the Supabase client (login only), and one Socket.IO clientThe host's login session (saved in the browser's local storage by supabase-js); React state for the current screen
VercelNothing runs. It only serves the files produced by npm run build, and its rewrite rule sends every URL to index.htmlNone
Renderserver/server.js: one Node.js process with Express and Socket.IO sharing one HTTP serverIn memory: the rooms Map (every live game) and the AI rate-limit log. Lost on restart
SupabasePostgres database, Auth service, and two Postgres functions (create_quiz, save_session_results)Permanent: host accounts, quizzes, questions, saved session results
GeminiThe language modelNone (each request is independent)
Key idea

The browser never talks to the database directly. It only uses Supabase for logging in. Every quiz read or write goes through the Render server, which checks who you are, validates the data, and only then uses its secret key to reach the database.

2.3 Layers inside the server

The server follows a common layered pattern. Each layer has one job and only calls the layer below it:

Figure 2.2: Server layers. REST requests enter through routes; live events enter through socket handlers. Both share the same services.
Real-life example

Think of a restaurant. The route is the host stand that sends you to the right table. The middleware is the bouncer checking your ID. The controller is the waiter who takes your order and checks it makes sense. The service is the kitchen that does the real work. The database is the pantry.

Where in the code
  • server/server.js: creates the HTTP server, attaches Express (src/app.js) and Socket.IO, and calls registerSocketHandler(io)
  • server/src/app.js: Express setup (CORS, JSON body parsing, routes)
  • client/src/main.jsx → App.jsx: the React entry point and routes
Interview tip

Draw figure 2.1 from memory: browser, Vercel, Render, Supabase, Gemini. Then explain the split: "Static files on a CDN, a long-running Node server for WebSockets, a managed Postgres for permanent data. I used Render instead of Vercel for the server because Vercel's serverless functions can't hold open WebSocket connections or keep game state in memory."

3.Concepts and technologies

This chapter defines every technical term in the guide, once, grouped by topic so you can revise a whole area at a time (for example, all the security terms before an interview). Everywhere else in the guide, a term with a dotted underline is a link back to its definition here. An alphabetical index of all terms is at the end of the guide.

Every term has the same four parts:

  • Definition: "In one sentence" is the version to say first in an interview; "In more detail" is the accurate follow-up.
  • Real-life example: an everyday comparison, with a note where it stops being accurate.
  • Where real apps use it: well-known places you will recognise.
  • Where in QUIZZY: the exact file and function in this project.
Interview tip

Answer "what is X?" in three moves: the one-sentence definition, one detail that shows you understand how it works, then "in my project, I used it for …". That last step is what makes your answer memorable.

3.1 Web basics

Client

Definition

In one sentence: The program a person actually uses (here, the QUIZZY website open in a browser) that asks a server for data and shows the results on screen.

In more detail: In web apps the client is usually a browser running HTML, CSS and JavaScript; a phone app is also a client. It handles what you see and click, and sends requests to a server when it needs data or wants something saved. Because the client runs on the user's own device, the user can inspect or even change it, so a client must never be trusted to enforce rules or security.

Real-life example

A customer in a restaurant: they read the menu and place orders, but the kitchen decides what actually gets cooked.

Where real apps use it
  • Web browsers showing Gmail or YouTube: the page you click on is the client.
  • Phone apps such as Instagram: the app on your phone is a client of Instagram's servers.
Where in QUIZZY

Everything in client/. client/src/main.jsx starts the React app in the browser, and pages such as PlayerPage.jsx send messages to the server and show what comes back.

Server

Definition

In one sentence: A program that waits for requests from clients, does the work (such as checking a password or saving data) and sends back an answer.

In more detail: A server usually runs on a computer in a data centre and serves many clients at the same time. It holds the things clients must not touch directly (the database, secret keys, the rules of the game) and decides what each client is allowed to do. "Server" can mean the program or the computer it runs on.

Real-life example

The kitchen of a restaurant: it takes orders from many tables, uses ingredients the customers never touch, and sends back finished dishes.

Where real apps use it
  • Google Search: your question is answered by Google's servers.
  • Online multiplayer games: a game server keeps every player's view of the match in sync.
Where in QUIZZY

server/server.js starts QUIZZY's server on Render. It answers REST requests (server/src/app.js) and runs the live game (server/src/sockets/socket.js).

Frontend

Definition

In one sentence: The part of an app that the user sees and interacts with: screens, buttons and forms.

In more detail: Frontend code is about presentation and interaction: layout, styling, reacting to clicks, and asking the backend for data. On the web it is written in HTML, CSS and JavaScript, often with a library such as React, and it runs in the browser. In everyday talk "frontend" and "client" are often used for the same thing; strictly, the frontend is the code and the client is the program running it.

Real-life example

The dining room of a restaurant: the decor, the menu and the waiters are everything the guests experience.

Where real apps use it
  • The Netflix screens where you browse and pick a film.
  • The forms of an online banking website.
Where in QUIZZY

Everything in client/src: the pages in client/src/pages and the components in client/src/components, built with React and Tailwind CSS.

Backend

Definition

In one sentence: The behind-the-scenes part of an app that stores data, applies the rules and talks to other services; users never see it directly.

In more detail: Backend code runs on servers. It usually offers an API to the frontend, checks the incoming data, decides who is allowed to do what, reads and writes the database, and calls outside services such as payments, email or AI. Keeping this logic in the backend means users can't tamper with it.

Real-life example

The kitchen, storeroom and accounts office of a restaurant together.

Where real apps use it
  • An online shop's backend charging your card and creating the order.
  • A ride-hailing app's backend matching riders with nearby drivers.
Where in QUIZZY

Everything in server/src: routes, controllers and services. For example, server/src/services/room.service.js → submitAnswer decides whether an answer is correct and updates the score.

API (Application Programming Interface)

Definition

In one sentence: A fixed menu of requests one program is allowed to make to another program, with clear rules for what to send and what comes back.

In more detail: An API hides how something works inside and only exposes agreed operations, such as "list my quizzes" or "generate questions". Web APIs are called over the internet using HTTP; code libraries also have APIs (the functions you can call). As long as the API stays the same, the inside can be rebuilt without breaking the programs that use it.

Real-life example

A restaurant menu: you order "dish 12" without knowing the recipe, and the kitchen can change cooks without changing the menu.

Where real apps use it
  • Weather apps getting forecasts from a weather service's API.
  • "Log in with Google" buttons, which use Google's sign-in API.
  • Checkout pages that take payments through a payment provider's API.
Where in QUIZZY

QUIZZY's server offers a REST API under /api/quizzes (server/src/routes/quiz.routes.js), and itself calls Gemini's API (server/src/services/ai.service.js) and Supabase's API (server/src/db/supaBase.js).

HTTP

Definition

In one sentence: The set of rules browsers and servers use to send each other requests and responses on the web.

In more detail: HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) works as request then response: the client sends a method (such as GET), a URL, headers and sometimes a body; the server replies with a status code, headers and a body. Each request stands on its own, because the server doesn't automatically remember earlier ones (HTTP is "stateless"). That is why a logged-in user's token is sent again with every request.

Real-life example

Ordering at a counter using a standard order form: every form gets exactly one reply slip, and the clerk doesn't remember your previous forms.

Where real apps use it
  • Every time a browser loads a web page.
  • Phone apps fetching your news feed or messages.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/api.js → apiFetch sends HTTP requests with fetch to the Express server set up in server/src/app.js.

HTTPS and TLS

Definition

In one sentence: HTTP with encryption (scrambling the data so only the intended receiver can read it), so nobody between the browser and the server can read or change what is sent.

In more detail: HTTPS is HTTP sent through TLS (Transport Layer Security). TLS encrypts the data and uses a certificate to prove the server really is the website it claims to be. The padlock in the address bar means HTTPS is in use. Without it, anyone on the same Wi-Fi network could read passwords or login tokens.

Real-life example

Sending letters in a locked box that only the recipient can open, delivered by a courier who first shows an official ID proving they work for the right company.

Where real apps use it
  • Online banking and shopping sites.
  • Every login page; today almost all websites use HTTPS.
Where in QUIZZY

Vercel and Render provide HTTPS automatically. Because VITE_API_URL starts with https://, client/src/api.js → apiFetch and both sockets travel encrypted. TLS is handled by Render's proxy, not by server/server.js.

URL

Definition

In one sentence: The full address of something on the web, such as https://example.com/join/483920.

In more detail: A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) has parts: the scheme (https), the domain (example.com), an optional port (:3000), the path (/join/483920) and sometimes a query string (?page=2). The path tells the server, or in a single-page application the router, what is being asked for.

Real-life example

A postal address: country, city, street and house number narrow down exactly where something is.

Where real apps use it
  • Links you share in chats and emails.
  • QR codes on posters and menus, which usually just contain a URL.
Where in QUIZZY

The QR code in the host lobby encodes joinLink, built in client/src/pages/HostPage.jsx as window.location.origin + "/join/" + roomCode; the router then reads the code from the path.

Origin

Definition

In one sentence: The "home address" of a web page: its scheme, domain and port together, for example https://quizzy.vercel.app.

In more detail: Two URLs have the same origin only if all three parts match: http versus https, a different subdomain, or a different port all count as different origins. Browsers use the origin as a security boundary called the same-origin policy: code from one origin can't read data from another origin unless that origin allows it through CORS.

Real-life example

Surname, street and house number together: two people are "from the same house" only if all three match.

Where real apps use it
  • Being logged in to your bank's site doesn't let another site you open read your account page, because they are different origins.
  • app.example.com and api.example.com are different origins, so the API must allow the app via CORS.
Where in QUIZZY

The Vercel site and the Render server are different origins. The CLIENT_URL variable tells server/src/app.js and server/server.js which origin to trust.

JSON

Definition

In one sentence: A simple text format for sending data between programs, written like {"title": "Planets", "count": 5}.

In more detail: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) can represent objects (named values in curly braces), lists (in square brackets), text, numbers, true/false and null. Almost every programming language can read and write it, so it is the common language of web APIs. In JavaScript, JSON.stringify turns data into JSON text and JSON.parse turns it back.

Real-life example

A standard shipping form that every courier in the world understands, whatever language they speak.

Where real apps use it
  • Most web APIs send and receive JSON.
  • Configuration files such as package.json in JavaScript projects.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/api.js → apiFetch sends request bodies as JSON, express.json() in server/src/app.js reads them, and server/src/services/ai.service.js → generateQuestions turns Gemini's answer into data with JSON.parse.

REST

Definition

In one sentence: A common style for designing web APIs in which every kind of thing has its own URL and standard HTTP methods are used to read or change it.

In more detail: REST (Representational State Transfer) organises an API around "resources", such as /api/quizzes, and uses HTTP methods as the actions: GET to read, POST to create, PUT or PATCH to update, DELETE to remove. Each request carries everything the server needs (including the login token), and results are reported with standard status codes. It is simple and works with ordinary web tools.

Real-life example

A library catalogue: every book has a shelf number (the URL), and the same few actions (look, borrow, return) work for every book.

Where real apps use it
  • Public developer APIs such as GitHub's, where for example a list of repositories has its own URL.
  • The backends of most phone apps.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/routes/quiz.routes.js: GET /api/quizzes lists quizzes, POST /api/quizzes creates one, GET /api/quizzes/:id reads one.

HTTP methods (GET and POST)

Definition

In one sentence: The verb of a web request: GET means "give me something", POST means "here is something new, please save or process it".

In more detail: A GET request only reads data, must not change anything, has no body, and can be repeated safely. A POST sends data in its body to create something or to trigger an action; sending it twice may create a duplicate. Other methods are PUT or PATCH (update) and DELETE (remove).

Real-life example

GET is asking a librarian to show you a book; POST is handing in a form to register a new book.

Where real apps use it
  • Opening any web page is a GET request.
  • Submitting a sign-up or checkout form is usually a POST request.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/pages/QuizListPage.jsx sends GET /api/quizzes; CreateQuizPage.jsx → handleSubmit sends POST /api/quizzes, and handleGenerate sends POST /api/quizzes/generate (a POST because it sends data and starts work).

HTTP status codes

Definition

In one sentence: A three-digit number in every response that says how the request went: 2xx means success, 4xx means the request had a problem, 5xx means the server had a problem.

In more detail: The client uses the code to decide what to do next: show the result, show an error, send the user to the login page, or try again later. Choosing the right code is part of designing a good API. The codes used in QUIZZY:

CodeNameMeaning in plain words
200OKHere is what you asked for.
201CreatedI made the new thing you sent.
400Bad RequestYour data is wrong or incomplete.
401UnauthorizedI don't know who you are (not logged in, or the token is invalid).
403ForbiddenI know who you are, but you may not do this.
404Not FoundThere is nothing here (or nothing you may see).
413Payload Too LargeWhat you sent is bigger than allowed.
429Too Many RequestsSlow down; try again later.
500Internal Server ErrorSomething broke on the server.
502Bad GatewayA service the server relies on failed.
Real-life example

The stamps on a returned parcel: "delivered", "address incomplete", "recipient unknown", "post office closed".

Where the analogy breaks down: Despite its name, 401 "Unauthorized" really means "not authenticated" (we don't know who you are); 403 is the real "not allowed".

Where real apps use it
  • The "404 Page not found" page on any website.
  • APIs answering 429 when you send too many requests.
  • "Something went wrong" pages, which usually come from a 500.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/controllers/quiz.controller.js picks the codes: createQuiz returns 201 or 400, getQuiz returns 404 for other hosts' quizzes, generateQuiz returns 502 when Gemini fails; requireAuth.js returns 401.

Request header

Definition

In one sentence: Extra labelled information sent along with a request, separate from its main content, such as "this is JSON" or "here is my login token".

In more detail: Headers are name and value pairs, for example Content-Type: application/json or Authorization: Bearer <token>. Servers read them to know how to handle the request. Responses have headers too, such as Access-Control-Allow-Origin for CORS or Retry-After after a 429.

Real-life example

The writing on the outside of an envelope (addressee, "fragile", return address), while the letter inside is the body.

Where real apps use it
  • Browsers send your preferred language so sites can show the right one.
  • APIs read the Authorization header to find out who is calling.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/api.js → apiFetch sets the Content-Type and Authorization headers; server/src/middlewares/requireAuth.js reads req.headers.authorization; aiRateLimit.js sets the Retry-After response header.

CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing)

Definition

In one sentence: A browser rule that stops a web page from reading data from a different website's server, unless that server says the page is allowed to.

In more detail: Browsers follow the "same-origin policy": JavaScript loaded from one origin can't read responses from another origin by default. CORS is how a server opts in: it sends response headers such as Access-Control-Allow-Origin naming the origins it trusts. This protects users, because a malicious site you visit can't use your browser, and your logins, to read data from another site. CORS is enforced only by browsers; tools such as curl ignore it, so it never replaces checking who the caller is.

Real-life example

A receptionist who only hands you a reply letter from another company if that company's letterhead says "OK to share with visitors from Vercel Street".

Where the analogy breaks down: The other company may already have received and acted on your request; CORS only controls whether the page gets to read the answer. That is why servers must still check permissions themselves.

Where real apps use it
  • A web app on app.example.com calling its own API on api.example.com, which allows exactly that origin.
  • Public data APIs such as weather services, which deliberately allow every origin.
  • Web fonts loaded from another domain, which need CORS headers to be usable.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/app.js → cors({ origin: CLIENT_URL }) and server/server.js → new Server(httpServer, { cors: { origin: CLIENT_URL } }) let only the Vercel site call the Render API and the Socket.IO server.

Preflight request

Definition

In one sentence: A short automatic "may I?" request the browser sends before certain cross-origin requests, to check that the server allows them.

In more detail: For cross-origin requests that aren't "simple", for example ones carrying an Authorization header or a JSON body, the browser first sends an OPTIONS request asking which methods and headers are allowed. Only if the server's CORS headers approve does the browser send the real request. Your own code never sends it; the browser does it by itself.

Real-life example

Phoning ahead to ask whether you may bring a guest, before turning up at the party.

Where real apps use it
  • Single-page apps calling an API on another domain with a login token.
  • Any fetch that sends JSON to a different origin.
Where in QUIZZY

Every client/src/api.js → apiFetch call from Vercel to Render triggers a preflight (it has an Authorization header and a JSON body); the cors middleware in server/src/app.js answers it.

Polling

Definition

In one sentence: Asking a server "anything new?" again and again on a timer.

In more detail: Polling is the simplest way to get updates over plain HTTP, but most requests come back with nothing new, which wastes data and battery, and every update waits until the next ask. Long-polling improves on it, and WebSockets avoid the problem by keeping one connection open so the server can speak first.

Real-life example

A child in the back seat asking "are we there yet?" every minute.

Where real apps use it
  • Older webmail pages checking for new mail every few minutes.
  • Simple dashboards that refresh their numbers every few seconds.
Where in QUIZZY

QUIZZY deliberately avoids polling: DECISIONS.md decision 4 rejects it in favour of Socket.IO, which only uses long-polling briefly while a connection starts.

CDN (Content Delivery Network)

Definition

In one sentence: A network of servers around the world that keep copies of a website's files, so each visitor downloads them from a server near them.

In more detail: CDN servers store (cache) static files such as HTML, JavaScript and images close to users. This makes pages load faster and protects the main server from traffic spikes. It suits files that are the same for everyone; personal or live data still comes from the app's own server.

Real-life example

A chain of local warehouses all stocking the same products, so every delivery comes from the closest one.

Where real apps use it
  • Video streaming services sending video from servers near the viewer.
  • News sites serving their images and scripts.
Where in QUIZZY

Vercel serves the built files from client/dist through its CDN; the live game data still comes from the server on Render.

Mixed content

Definition

In one sentence: When a secure (HTTPS) page tries to load something over insecure HTTP; browsers block it.

In more detail: If an HTTPS page fetched data over plain http:// or ws://, that part could be read or changed on the way, breaking the page's promise of security. Browsers therefore block such requests. The fix is to use https:// and wss:// for everything.

Real-life example

A bank vault with its back door left open, so the guard locks the back door before letting anything through.

Where real apps use it
  • Old websites that moved to HTTPS but still loaded images over http://.
  • A deployed HTTPS site accidentally calling http://localhost.
Where in QUIZZY

VITE_API_URL (read in client/src/config/config.js) must start with https:// on Vercel; an http:// value would make the browser block every apiFetch call and both sockets.

3.2 Real-time communication

Real-time

Definition

In one sentence: Updates appear on your screen the moment something happens, without anyone refreshing the page.

In more detail: A real-time web app keeps a live connection open so the server can push changes immediately, usually within a fraction of a second. This needs a connection that stays open, such as a WebSocket, and the server must keep track of who should receive each update.

Real-life example

Watching a football match live instead of reading about it in tomorrow's newspaper.

Where real apps use it
  • Chat apps showing new messages instantly.
  • Live sports scores.
  • Delivery and ride-tracking maps that move the car as it drives.
Where in QUIZZY

The host's leaderboard (client/src/components/Leaderboard.jsx) changes as soon as server/src/sockets/socket.js → emitLeaderboard runs after a student answers.

WebSocket

Definition

In one sentence: A connection between a browser and a server that stays open, so either side can send messages at any moment.

In more detail: A normal HTTP request is one question and one answer, and then it's finished. A WebSocket starts as an HTTP request and is then "upgraded" into a long-lived, two-way connection. This lets the server push updates instantly instead of the browser asking again and again (polling).

Real-life example

HTTP is like sending letters; a WebSocket is like a phone call that stays connected, where either person can speak whenever they want.

Where real apps use it
  • Chat apps like WhatsApp Web: new messages appear instantly.
  • Collaborative editors like Google Docs: you see others typing.
  • Live sports scores and trading dashboards.
Where in QUIZZY

Socket.IO uses WebSockets for the live game. server/src/sockets/socket.js handles events such as quiz:answer, and the host's leaderboard updates the moment any student answers.

Long-polling

Definition

In one sentence: A way to get near-instant updates over normal HTTP: the browser asks for news, and the server holds the question open until there is something to say.

In more detail: When the server finally answers (or a time limit passes), the browser immediately asks again. It works on any network that allows normal web traffic, even ones that block WebSockets, but every message costs a full HTTP request. Socket.IO starts every connection with long-polling and switches ("upgrades") to a WebSocket when it can.

Real-life example

Asking a shopkeeper to call you back when your parcel arrives, and phoning again right after each call.

Where real apps use it
  • Chat systems falling back to it on strict company or school networks.
  • Real-time web apps from before WebSockets were widely supported.
Where in QUIZZY

socket.io-client (client/src/socket/socket.js, client/src/hostSocket.js) starts with long-polling and then upgrades; those first ordinary HTTP requests are why the Socket.IO server in server/server.js needs CORS settings.

WSS (secure WebSocket)

Definition

In one sentence: A WebSocket connection protected by encryption: the WebSocket version of HTTPS.

In more detail: wss:// is a WebSocket sent through TLS, exactly as https:// is HTTP sent through TLS. A page loaded over HTTPS must use wss://, otherwise the browser blocks the connection as mixed content. With Socket.IO you don't type wss:// yourself: giving it an https:// address makes it use wss://.

Real-life example

The same phone call as a WebSocket, but on a scrambled line that eavesdroppers can't understand.

Where real apps use it
  • WhatsApp Web and other browser chat apps.
  • Online trading platforms streaming live prices.
Where in QUIZZY

Because VITE_API_URL starts with https://, the sockets in client/src/socket/socket.js and client/src/hostSocket.js connect to Render with wss://.

Socket.IO

Definition

In one sentence: A library that makes real-time messaging between browsers and a server easy, built on top of WebSockets.

In more detail: Socket.IO adds features plain WebSockets don't have: named events, socket rooms for sending to groups, automatic reconnection, acknowledgements, and a fallback to long-polling. It has two halves, socket.io on the Node server and socket.io-client in the browser, and both sides must use Socket.IO: a plain WebSocket client can't talk to a Socket.IO server.

Real-life example

A walkie-talkie system with labelled channels, automatic reconnection when you walk back into range, and "message received" confirmations.

Where real apps use it
  • Chat features in web apps.
  • Live dashboards and notifications.
  • Multiplayer browser games.
Where in QUIZZY

server/server.js creates the Socket.IO server, server/src/sockets/socket.js → registerSocketHandler registers every event, and the browser clients are in client/src/socket/socket.js and client/src/hostSocket.js.

Why QUIZZY uses Socket.IO: the host's screen must update when other people act (a student joins, a student answers). With plain HTTP, the host's browser would have to keep polling. DECISIONS.md decision 4 records this choice and rejects polling.

Event

Definition

In one sentence: A named message that says "this just happened", which code can listen for and react to.

In more detail: In Socket.IO an event has a name, such as quiz:answer, and optional data. One side sends it; the other side runs the function registered for that name with socket.on(name, handler). Some events, like connect and disconnect, are sent by Socket.IO itself. Browsers use the same idea for clicks and key presses.

Real-life example

A doorbell: pressing it sends one specific signal, and whoever is listening decides what to do about it.

Where real apps use it
  • Chat apps sending "new message" and "is typing" events.
  • Online games sending "player moved" events.
  • Every web page reacting to click events.
Where in QUIZZY

QUIZZY has 20 custom events (section 6.8). For example, client/src/pages/PlayerPage.jsx → handleAnswer sends quiz:answer, and server/src/sockets/socket.js handles it with socket.on("quiz:answer", …).

Emit

Definition

In one sentence: To send an event.

In more detail: socket.emit(name, data) sends an event over one connection: from the browser to the server, or from the server back to that one browser. To send to many connections at once, the server uses io.to(…).emit(…). An emit can also carry a callback to receive an acknowledgement.

Real-life example

Saying something into one particular phone call.

Where real apps use it
  • A chat app emitting "new message" when you press send.
  • A game emitting your move to the server.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/pages/PlayerPage.jsx → handleAnswer emits quiz:answer; the server's quiz:answer handler in server/src/sockets/socket.js replies with socket.emit("quiz:answer:result", …).

Socket room

Definition

In one sentence: A named group of live connections on the server, so one message can be sent to everyone in the group at once.

In more detail: In Socket.IO, socket.join(name) adds a connection to a socket room and io.to(name).emit(…) sends to all of its members. Socket rooms exist only on the server (browsers don't know which rooms they are in), and every connection is automatically in a room named after its own socket ID. In this guide, "socket room" always means this Socket.IO group, while "room" means QUIZZY's own game room object in memory.

Real-life example

A group chat: post once and every member receives it, and only the admin (the server) adds or removes members.

Where real apps use it
  • Chat channels, with one socket room per channel.
  • Collaborative editors, with one socket room per open document.
  • Online games, with one socket room per match.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/sockets/socket.js puts every socket of a game into the socket room "483920" and the host's sockets also into "host:483920"; io.to(player.id) uses each player's personal socket room.

Broadcast

Definition

In one sentence: Sending one message to many receivers at the same time.

In more detail: In Socket.IO you broadcast by emitting to a socket room (io.to(room).emit) or to every connection (io.emit). The server sends a copy to each member; connections that aren't targeted receive nothing, so choosing the right socket room decides who sees what.

Real-life example

A loudspeaker announcement in one classroom: everyone in that room hears it, nobody in the next room does.

Where real apps use it
  • A new message delivered to all members of a group chat.
  • A goal update pushed to everyone watching a match.
Where in QUIZZY

The player:join handler in server/src/sockets/socket.js broadcasts room:players to the whole game with io.to(room.code).emit, while emitLeaderboard broadcasts only to "host:CODE".

Acknowledgement

Definition

In one sentence: A reply that confirms "I got your message and dealt with it".

In more detail: In Socket.IO the sender adds a callback function as the last argument of emit; the receiver calls it when finished, and the callback then runs on the sender's side, optionally with data. socket.timeout(ms).emit(…) adds a deadline: if no acknowledgement (often shortened to "ack") arrives in time, the callback receives an error instead. It turns "send and hope" into "send and get confirmation".

Real-life example

Recorded delivery: you get a signature back once the parcel has arrived.

Where real apps use it
  • The "delivered" ticks in messaging apps.
  • An app saving a document and showing "Saved" only after the server confirms.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/pages/HostPage.jsx → handleCloseRoom uses socket.timeout(3000).emit("host:close-room", …); the server's host:close-room handler calls the acknowledgement after closing the room, and the page then goes to /host.

Handshake

Definition

In one sentence: The first exchange when a connection is opened, in which both sides agree to talk and the client can show its credentials.

In more detail: For a WebSocket, the handshake is an HTTP request asking to "upgrade" the connection. Socket.IO adds its own handshake data: whatever the client puts in its auth option arrives on the server as socket.handshake.auth, and server-side middleware can check it before the connection is accepted.

Real-life example

Showing your ticket at the door before you are let into a concert.

Where real apps use it
  • Chat apps logging in to their server when they connect.
  • Every HTTPS connection, which starts with a TLS handshake to agree on encryption.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/hostSocket.js sends { token } in the handshake; server/src/sockets/socketAuth.js → socketAuth reads socket.handshake.auth.token and stores the user's ID in socket.data.userId.

Reconnection

Definition

In one sentence: Automatically connecting again after a connection drops, without the user doing anything.

In more detail: Socket.IO clients keep retrying, with growing pauses, when the connection is lost, for example after Wi-Fi drops or the server restarts. A reconnected client is a brand-new connection with a new socket ID, so the app must restore its own situation, for example by telling the server again who it is.

Real-life example

Your phone automatically redialling after a call drops, but the person on the other end still has to recognise your voice.

Where real apps use it
  • Chat apps coming back online after you leave a tunnel.
  • Video calls that freeze for a moment and then resume.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/pages/HostPage.jsx listens for connect (handleConnect), so after every reconnection it sends host:resume and server/src/sockets/socket.js re-attaches the host to their room. Students have no equivalent yet (section 14).

3.3 React and the browser

Component

Definition

In one sentence: A reusable piece of the user interface, written as a function that returns what should appear on screen.

In more detail: In React, a component is a JavaScript function whose name starts with a capital letter and that returns JSX. Components can contain other components, so a whole page is a tree of small pieces. A component receives inputs as props and can remember its own state; React runs the function again whenever either of them changes.

Real-life example

LEGO bricks: small standard pieces, each with one shape, combined into bigger structures and reused in many builds.

Where real apps use it
  • Social media feeds, where every post, like button and comment box is a component used thousands of times.
  • Design systems that give a company one shared set of buttons, cards and inputs.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/components/QuestionView.jsx is a component used by PlayerPage; client/src/components/Button.jsx is used by all six pages.

JSX

Definition

In one sentence: The HTML-like code you write inside JavaScript to describe what a React component shows.

In more detail: JSX looks like HTML, for example <Button onClick={handleJoin}>Join</Button>, but the build tool turns it into ordinary JavaScript function calls. Curly braces { } insert JavaScript values. Small differences from HTML include className instead of class and event names in camelCase, like onClick. Text inserted with { } is escaped automatically, which protects against XSS.

Real-life example

A fill-in-the-blanks letter template: the layout is fixed, and the gaps in curly braces are filled with live data.

Where real apps use it
  • Every React web app.
  • React Native phone apps, which use the same JSX syntax.
Where in QUIZZY

Every .jsx file. For example, client/src/pages/PlayerPage.jsx returns different JSX for each screen of the game.

Props

Definition

In one sentence: The inputs you pass into a component, like the settings you give a function when you call it.

In more detail: Props are written like HTML attributes, for example <QuestionView data={currentQuestion} disabled={…} />, and the component receives them as one object. Props flow one way, from parent to child, and a child can't change its own props. To report something back, a parent passes a function as a prop (like onAnswer) that the child calls.

Real-life example

Ordering a pizza: you choose the size and toppings, and the kitchen makes what you described, but it can't change your order form.

Where real apps use it
  • A "like" button component given a post ID and the current number of likes.
  • A product card given a name, price and image.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/pages/PlayerPage.jsx passes data, selectedOption, correctOption, disabled and onAnswer to client/src/components/QuestionView.jsx.

State (in React)

Definition

In one sentence: Data a component remembers between screen updates; when it changes, React redraws that part of the screen.

In more detail: State is created with useState and belongs to one component on screen. Unlike a normal variable, it keeps its value when the component runs again, and changing it through its setter function tells React to redraw. Anything on screen that changes over time (typed text, the current question, the score) is driven by state.

Real-life example

The scoreboard at a match: when someone changes the number, everyone looking at it sees the new score.

Where real apps use it
  • The item count on a shopping cart icon.
  • A dark-mode on/off switch.
  • The unread badge on a notifications bell.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/pages/PlayerPage.jsx keeps nickname, joined, currentQuestion, result, score, finished and more in state.

Hook

Definition

In one sentence: A special React function, whose name starts with "use", that gives a component a React feature such as memory (state) or running code after drawing (effects).

In more detail: Built-in hooks include useState, useEffect and useContext. They must be called at the top level of a component, in the same order every time, never inside if statements or loops, because React tells them apart by their order. You can also combine hooks into your own custom hooks.

Real-life example

Standard sockets in a wall: plug an appliance (the component) into the right socket to get power (state or effects), and the sockets must always be in the same place.

Where the analogy breaks down: Real sockets can be used in any order; hooks can't, which is exactly the rule that trips beginners up.

Where real apps use it
  • All modern React apps.
  • Libraries that offer hooks, such as useNavigate from React Router.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/pages/PlayerPage.jsx uses useState, useEffect and useParams; QuizListPage.jsx uses the custom hook useAuth.

useState

Definition

In one sentence: The hook that gives a component a piece of state plus a function to change it.

In more detail: const [score, setScore] = useState(0) returns the current value and a setter. Calling setScore(10) asks React to redraw with the new value. When the new value depends on the old one, pass a function instead, for example setQuestions(prev => [...prev, q]), so you always build on the latest value.

Real-life example

A whiteboard with a marker: anyone can read it, the marker is the only way to change it, and everyone watching sees the update.

Where real apps use it
  • Opening and closing a menu.
  • The text inside a search box.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/pages/CreateQuizPage.jsx keeps title, questions, saving and generating with useState; addQuestion calls setQuestions((prev) => [...prev, emptyQuestion()]).

useEffect

Definition

In one sentence: The hook for running code after the screen has been drawn, usually to connect to something outside React.

In more detail: useEffect(fn, deps) runs fn after drawing; with an empty list [] as deps, it runs once when the component first appears. It is used for "side effects": loading data, starting timers, subscribing to updates, opening sockets. The function can return a cleanup function to undo what it started.

Real-life example

Moving into a flat: once you're in, you set up the internet and mail forwarding (the effect); when you move out, you cancel them (the cleanup).

Where real apps use it
  • Loading data when a page opens.
  • Subscribing to live updates, such as a chat connection.
  • Changing the browser tab's title.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/pages/PlayerPage.jsx registers its socket listeners and calls socket.connect() inside useEffect; QuizListPage.jsx loads the quiz list in one.

Cleanup function

Definition

In one sentence: The function a useEffect returns, which React runs to undo the effect when the component disappears (or before the effect runs again).

In more detail: It removes listeners, clears timers and closes connections so they don't keep running after the screen is gone. Forgetting it causes memory leaks and duplicated behaviour, for example every event being handled twice after you navigate away and back.

Real-life example

Switching off the lights and locking the door when you leave a room.

Where real apps use it
  • Closing a chat connection when you leave a chat screen.
  • Stopping a countdown timer when a dialog closes.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/pages/PlayerPage.jsx and HostPage.jsx return a function that calls socket.off(…) for every listener and then socket.disconnect(); QuizListPage.jsx's cleanup sets ignore = true so a late answer is ignored.

Context (React)

Definition

In one sentence: A React feature for sharing data with many components without passing it by hand through every level in between.

In more detail: A Provider component high up in the tree supplies a value, and any component below it can read that value with useContext or a custom hook. It avoids "prop drilling", which means passing the same prop through components that don't need it. It suits app-wide data such as the logged-in user or the colour theme.

Real-life example

A building's Wi-Fi: every room can connect directly, instead of running a cable through every room in between.

Where real apps use it
  • Logged-in user information shown on every page.
  • Light and dark themes.
  • Language settings.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/auth/AuthContext.jsx → AuthProvider wraps the whole app in client/src/main.jsx and shares session, user, loading and signOut.

Custom hook

Definition

In one sentence: Your own function, whose name starts with "use", that bundles up hooks you need in several places.

In more detail: A custom hook can call other hooks and return whatever is useful. It shares logic, not data: each component that calls it gets its own values, unless the hook reads something shared such as a context. It keeps components short and puts the shared logic in one place.

Real-life example

A recipe card you reuse: every cook who follows it makes their own dish.

Where real apps use it
  • Common app hooks such as "use the current user" or "use the window size".
  • Library hooks such as useNavigate and useParams from React Router.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/auth/AuthContext.jsx → useAuth reads the auth context and throws a clear error if it is used outside AuthProvider; RequireAuth, LoginPage and QuizListPage use it.

Controlled input

Definition

In one sentence: A form field whose content always comes from React state, so React decides what it shows.

In more detail: You set value={nickname} and update the state in onChange. Every keystroke goes through your code, so you can check or change it (for example, remove anything that isn't a digit), and the state always matches what's on screen. The alternative, an uncontrolled input, keeps its own value inside the browser.

Real-life example

A puppet: it only moves when the puppeteer (the state) pulls the strings.

Where real apps use it
  • Search boxes that filter results as you type.
  • Card number fields that add spaces as you type.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/pages/HomePage.jsx uses onChange={(e) => setCode(e.target.value.replace(/\D/g, ""))} so only digits appear; the nickname field in PlayerPage.jsx is controlled by nickname.

Conditional rendering

Definition

In one sentence: Showing different things on screen depending on a condition.

In more detail: In JSX you use normal JavaScript: {error && <ErrorMessage>…} shows the message only when error has a value, and condition ? <A /> : <B /> picks one of two. Because React shows exactly what the expression produces, the screen always matches the state.

Real-life example

A shop sign that shows OPEN or CLOSED depending on the time.

Where real apps use it
  • Showing "Log in" or your profile picture depending on whether you are logged in.
  • Showing a loading spinner until the content arrives.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/pages/HostPage.jsx shows the "End quiz" button only when leaderboard.status === "playing"; PlayerPage.jsx shows ErrorMessage only when error is set.

Early return

Definition

In one sentence: Leaving a function as soon as you know the answer, instead of wrapping everything in nested if/else blocks.

In more detail: In a component, if (loading) return <Spinner />; returns that screen right away and skips the rest. A row of early returns reads as "the first matching case wins". The same pattern in handlers (if (!valid) return;) keeps the main path of the code flat and easy to follow.

Real-life example

A bouncer going down a checklist: "banned? leave. no ticket? leave. otherwise, come in."

Where real apps use it
  • Route guards that send logged-out users to the login page.
  • Server handlers that stop at the first invalid input.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/pages/PlayerPage.jsx checks finalResult, closedMessage, finished, currentQuestion and joined in order and returns the first matching screen; server/src/services/room.service.js → addPlayer returns { error } early for each broken rule.

Key (in lists)

Definition

In one sentence: A unique label you give each item in a list so React can tell the items apart when the list changes.

In more detail: When you draw a list with map, each element needs key={…}. React uses keys to match old and new items, so it updates, moves or removes the right ones and keeps each item's state. Use a stable ID; using the position in the array mixes items up when the list is reordered, which also breaks animations.

Real-life example

Name tags at a party: people can move around the room, but you still know who is who.

Where real apps use it
  • Chat message lists.
  • Social media feeds and to-do lists.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/components/Leaderboard.jsx uses key={player.id} so rows slide to their new rank; CreateQuizPage.jsx uses the temporary q.id made by crypto.randomUUID().

Immutable update

Definition

In one sentence: Changing data by making an updated copy, instead of editing the original.

In more detail: React decides whether to redraw by checking whether the state is a new object or array. Editing an array in place (with push) keeps the same array, so React may not notice. Instead, create a new one with the spread operator or map: [...prev, item] or prev.map(…). It also prevents bugs where shared data changes unexpectedly.

Real-life example

Saving a new version of a document instead of writing over the old one, so anyone can see that something changed.

Where real apps use it
  • Undo and redo history in editors.
  • State-management libraries such as Redux, which require it.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/pages/CreateQuizPage.jsx → updateQuestion and updateOption use map and spread to return new arrays and objects.

Single-page application (SPA)

Definition

In one sentence: A website that loads one page once and then changes what's on screen with JavaScript, instead of loading a new page from the server for every click.

In more detail: The browser downloads index.html and the JavaScript bundle once; after that, moving between "pages" just swaps components, and data comes from API calls. This feels fast, like an app. The trade-off: the host must answer every path with index.html, or direct links like /join/483920 break.

Real-life example

A presenter at a whiteboard who erases and redraws parts of it, instead of handing out a new sheet of paper for every change.

Where real apps use it
  • Gmail.
  • Google Maps.
  • Project boards such as Trello.
Where in QUIZZY

client/index.html loads client/src/main.jsx once, and client/vercel.json sends every path to index.html.

Client-side routing

Definition

In one sentence: Switching pages inside a single-page application by changing the address bar and swapping components, without asking the server for a new page.

In more detail: A router library reads the path in the URL, shows the matching component, and updates the address bar when you navigate, using the browser's History API, so the back and forward buttons and bookmarks still work.

Real-life example

A receptionist directing visitors to different rooms inside the same building, so nobody has to leave and come back in.

Where real apps use it
  • Gmail moving between the inbox and a message.
  • Video sites moving to the next video without a full reload.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/App.jsx declares the routes with React Router; client/src/pages/HomePage.jsx → handleJoin calls navigate(`/join/${cleanCode}`).

URL parameter

Definition

In one sentence: A changeable part of a URL path, like the 483920 in /join/483920.

In more detail: A route is declared with a placeholder, such as /join/:code; the router accepts any value in that position and hands it to the component, in React Router through useParams(). One page can then show many different items.

Real-life example

The flat number in an address: every flat in the building has the same layout, but the number says which one you mean.

Where real apps use it
  • Product pages such as /product/123.
  • Profile pages such as /user/alice.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/pages/PlayerPage.jsx reads const { code } = useParams(); HostPage.jsx reads quizId the same way.

State machine

Definition

In one sentence: A way of describing something that is always in exactly one of a few named states, with clear rules for moving from one state to another.

In more detail: Each state allows certain events, and each event leads to a specific next state. Describing screens or game logic this way rules out impossible combinations, such as being "finished" and "waiting" at the same time, and makes the logic easy to draw as a diagram.

Real-life example

A traffic light: red, then green, then amber, then red again, and never two colours at once.

Where real apps use it
  • Order tracking: placed, shipped, delivered.
  • Media players: playing, paused, stopped.
Where in QUIZZY

A room's status goes "waiting" → "playing" → "finished" (server/src/services/room.service.js → startQuiz, endQuiz); the screens of PlayerPage.jsx form another state machine (figure 5.1).

localStorage

Definition

In one sentence: A small storage area in the browser where a website can keep text that is still there after the page or browser is closed.

In more detail: Data is stored per origin as name and value text, and survives reloads and restarts until it is cleared. Any JavaScript running on that origin can read it, so it must not hold anything an XSS attack shouldn't steal. sessionStorage works the same way but is emptied when the tab closes.

Real-life example

A locker at your gym: your things stay there between visits, but anyone who gets into that changing room can open it.

Where real apps use it
  • Remembering your dark-mode choice.
  • Keeping an unsent draft.
  • Many single-page apps storing the login session.
Where in QUIZZY

supabase-js (client/src/supabase/supabaseClient.js) keeps the host's session in localStorage, which is why refreshing the page doesn't log the host out.

Reduced motion

Definition

In one sentence: A setting on phones and computers that asks apps to use less animation, which websites can detect and respect.

In more detail: Movement on screen can make some people dizzy or distract them. Operating systems offer a "reduce motion" option, which CSS can detect with the prefers-reduced-motion media query. Considerate apps turn off or simplify animations when it is on, while still showing the same information.

Real-life example

A "no flash photography" sign at a show: the show goes on, just without the part that hurts some people.

Where real apps use it
  • iPhone and Android system animations.
  • Websites switching off moving backgrounds and parallax scrolling.
Where in QUIZZY

Tailwind's motion-reduce: classes (for example in client/src/components/Button.jsx) and <MotionConfig reducedMotion="user"> in client/src/components/Leaderboard.jsx.

3.4 JavaScript and Node.js

Runtime

Definition

In one sentence: The program that actually runs your code and gives it access to things like the network, files and timers.

In more detail: JavaScript always needs a runtime. A browser is one: it adds the web page, fetch and localStorage. Node.js is another: it adds files, network servers and process.env. The language is the same, but the built-in tools differ, which is why browser code can't read files from your disk and server code has no web page to draw on.

Real-life example

A games console: the game only runs on a console that supports it, and each console offers different controllers.

Where real apps use it
  • Web browsers, which run the JavaScript of every website.
  • Node.js, which runs web servers and developer tools (Vite itself runs on Node).
Where in QUIZZY

The code in client/ runs in the browser's runtime; server/server.js runs in Node.js on Render.

Event loop

Definition

In one sentence: The mechanism that lets JavaScript, which does one thing at a time, keep many tasks going by running each small job in turn instead of waiting.

In more detail: JavaScript runs one piece of code at a time. Slow operations (network calls, timers, database queries) are handed off; when they finish, the code that should handle the result is put in a queue, and the event loop runs queued jobs one by one whenever the current code has finished. Code is never interrupted in the middle, but one slow calculation blocks everything else.

Real-life example

A single chef who puts dishes in the oven and serves other orders while they cook, returning when each timer rings. But if the chef spends ten minutes chopping onions, nobody else gets served.

Where real apps use it
  • Node.js web servers handling thousands of connections with one thread.
  • Browsers keeping a page responsive while data loads.
Where in QUIZZY

The handlers in server/src/sockets/socket.js for many students run one at a time on Node's event loop, so two handlers never change the rooms Map at the same instant.

Asynchronous code

Definition

In one sentence: Code that starts a slow task, carries on with other work, and deals with the result later when it is ready.

In more detail: Network requests, database queries and timers take time; waiting for them would freeze the program. Asynchronous functions return straight away and deliver their result later, through callbacks, Promises or async/await. Anything after an await may run after other events have happened in between.

Real-life example

Ordering coffee and getting a buzzer: you sit down, and the buzzer tells you when your coffee is ready.

Where real apps use it
  • A feed loading more posts while you keep scrolling.
  • Photos uploading in the background while you use the app.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/api.js → apiFetch and server/src/services/quiz.service.js → getQuizById are asynchronous; the host:create-room handler in server/src/sockets/socket.js waits for the database with await.

Promise

Definition

In one sentence: An object that stands for a result that isn't ready yet, which will later either succeed with a value or fail with an error.

In more detail: A Promise starts as "pending" and then becomes "fulfilled" (with a value) or "rejected" (with an error). You say what should happen next with .then and .catch, or wait for it with await. fetch, Supabase queries and Gemini calls all return Promises.

Real-life example

A cloakroom ticket: it isn't your coat, but a promise that you'll get your coat back, or be told it's been lost.

Where real apps use it
  • Every fetch call in web apps.
  • Database and payment libraries that answer later.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/services/ai.service.js → sleep returns a Promise that finishes after a delay; client/src/auth/AuthContext.jsx uses supabase.auth.getSession().then(…).

async/await

Definition

In one sentence: Two keywords that let you write asynchronous code that reads top to bottom like normal code.

In more detail: async marks a function that returns a Promise; inside it, await pauses that function until a Promise finishes, without freezing the rest of the program. Errors from an awaited Promise can be caught with an ordinary try/catch.

Real-life example

A recipe step "wait until the dough has risen, then shape it": you can do other chores while you wait.

Where real apps use it
  • Modern Node.js servers.
  • Modern browser code that loads data.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/pages/CreateQuizPage.jsx → handleSubmit uses await apiFetch(…) inside try/catch/finally; server/src/middlewares/requireAuth.js awaits supabase.auth.getUser.

Module (import and export)

Definition

In one sentence: A single code file that shares chosen pieces with other files (export) and uses pieces from other files (import).

In more detail: Modules keep code organised and private by default: only what a file exports can be used elsewhere. The client uses ES modules (import/export); the server uses CommonJS (require/module.exports). A default export is a file's main item (import Button from "./Button"); named exports are imported in curly braces (import { apiFetch } from "./api").

Real-life example

Departments in a company: each keeps its own work private and shares only official documents with the others.

Where real apps use it
  • Every modern JavaScript project.
  • npm packages, which are modules other people publish.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/api.js has a named export apiFetch; server/src/services/room.service.js shares its functions with module.exports = { … } and server/src/sockets/socket.js loads them with require.

npm package (dependency)

Definition

In one sentence: Ready-made code published by other people that you add to your project instead of writing it yourself.

In more detail: npm is Node's package manager. package.json lists the packages a project depends on (its dependencies) with allowed version ranges; npm install downloads them into node_modules, and package-lock.json records the exact versions so every install is identical. devDependencies are only needed while developing and building.

Real-life example

Buying flat-pack furniture parts instead of cutting the wood yourself, with a parts list (package.json) that says exactly what you need.

Where real apps use it
  • React and Express are both npm packages.
  • Almost every JavaScript project uses dozens of them.
Where in QUIZZY

client/package.json lists packages such as react, socket.io-client, motion and qrcode.react; server/package.json lists express, socket.io, zod and @google/genai.

Singleton

Definition

In one sentence: Something that exists only once in the whole program, shared by every part of the code that uses it.

In more detail: In JavaScript, a module's code runs only once, so an object created at the top of a module and exported is in effect a singleton: every file that imports it gets the same object. It suits shared connections and clients. The downside is shared state, which can make code harder to test.

Real-life example

A school's single main office: everyone goes to the same place.

Where real apps use it
  • One shared database connection pool in a web server.
  • One app-wide logger.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/socket/socket.js and client/src/hostSocket.js each export one socket, server/src/db/supaBase.js exports one Supabase client, and server/src/services/room.service.js keeps one rooms Map.

Environment variable

Definition

In one sentence: A named setting given to a program from outside its code, such as GEMINI_API_KEY.

In more detail: The same code can then use different values on your laptop (from a .env file) and in production (from the Vercel or Render dashboard), and secrets never end up in Git. Node reads them from process.env; Vite exposes only variables whose names start with VITE_ to browser code, and bakes their values into the files at build time.

Real-life example

The thermostat settings in a rented flat: the flat (the code) is the same for every tenant, but each tenant sets their own temperature.

Where real apps use it
  • Every deployed web app, for database addresses and API keys.
  • Switching between test and live payment accounts without changing code.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/services/ai.service.js reads process.env.GEMINI_API_KEY; client/src/config/config.js reads import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL. Section 10.3 lists them all.

Map (JavaScript)

Definition

In one sentence: A JavaScript collection that stores values under keys, so you can look a value up quickly by its key.

In more detail: A Map holds key-and-value pairs with the methods set, get, has and delete; looking something up by key stays fast however many entries there are. Unlike a plain object, any type can be a key and the order of insertion is kept; unlike an array, you don't have to search through the items one by one.

Real-life example

A cloakroom: hand in ticket number 42 and you get exactly your coat back, straight away.

Where real apps use it
  • Caches that remember recent results.
  • Tracking which users are online, by user ID.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/services/room.service.js → const rooms = new Map() maps a room code to its room; server/src/middlewares/aiRateLimit.js maps each user ID to a list of times.

Pure function

Definition

In one sentence: A function whose result depends only on its inputs and which changes nothing outside itself.

In more detail: Given the same inputs, a pure function always returns the same output, and it has no "side effects": no network calls, no saving, no changing shared data. That makes it easy to test and reason about. Real programs mix pure logic with a few impure edges that talk to the outside world.

Real-life example

A calculator: 2 + 2 is always 4, and pressing the keys doesn't change anything else.

Where real apps use it
  • Price and tax calculations.
  • Formatting dates and numbers for display.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/services/question.service.js → getPublicQuestion and isCorrect, and quiz.service.js → toQuiz. The functions in room.service.js are not pure, because they change the rooms Map.

Destructuring

Definition

In one sentence: A shortcut for taking values out of an object or array and putting them into separate variables in one line.

In more detail: const { roomCode, nickname } = data creates two variables from data's properties; const [score, setScore] = useState(0) does the same for an array. You can rename values and give defaults. If the value being destructured is undefined or null, JavaScript throws an error, which is why defaults matter.

Real-life example

Unpacking a delivery box and putting each item straight onto its own shelf.

Where real apps use it
  • Reading fields from API responses.
  • Function parameters in React components (({ players, nickname })).
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/sockets/socket.js: socket.on("player:join", (data = {}) => { const { roomCode, nickname } = data; … }). The quiz:start handler destructures without a default, which is the cause of the crash in section 14.

Spread operator

Definition

In one sentence: Three dots (...) that copy all the items of an array, or all the properties of an object, into a new one.

In more detail: [...prev, item] makes a new array with one extra item; { ...q, text } copies an object and replaces text. When two objects are spread into one, properties written later win. The copy is shallow: objects nested inside are shared, not copied. It is the usual way to write immutable updates in React.

Real-life example

Photocopying a form and changing one field on the copy.

Where real apps use it
  • React state updates.
  • Merging a user's settings over the default settings.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/api.js → apiFetch spreads options and headers; server/src/controllers/quiz.controller.js → createQuiz spreads result.data, where the order matters (section 14).

3.5 Server design

Middleware

Definition

In one sentence: A checkpoint that every request passes through before it reaches the code that answers it, which can inspect the request, add information to it, or turn it away.

In more detail: In Express, a middleware is a function (req, res, next) that runs, in the order it was registered, before the route's handler. It can stop the request by replying itself (for example 401 "Not logged in"), attach facts to it (such as req.user), or call next() to pass it along. This lets you write a check like "is this user logged in?" once and apply it to many routes. Socket.IO uses the same idea for new connections with io.use(…).

Real-life example

Airport security before your gate: you pass the checkpoints in a fixed order (ID check, then bag scan), any of them can send you back, and the ID desk stamps your boarding pass so the gate doesn't have to check your ID again. That stamp is what requireAuth does when it sets req.user.

Where real apps use it
  • Almost every web backend, to check the login on protected API routes.
  • Request logging, recording the path and response time of every request.
  • Reading JSON bodies and adding security headers.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/middlewares/requireAuth.js → requireAuth, applied to every quiz route by router.use(requireAuth) in quiz.routes.js, checks the Bearer token and sets req.user; server/src/sockets/socketAuth.js → socketAuth does the same job for socket connections.

Route

Definition

In one sentence: A rule that connects a web address and HTTP method to the code that should handle it.

In more detail: In Express, router.get("/", handler) means "GET requests to this path go to this handler". Paths can contain parameters such as /:id. Express checks routes in the order they were registered and stops at the first one that sends a response, which matters in QUIZZY (section 14, issue 2).

Real-life example

The signs in a hospital corridor that send each patient to the right department.

Where real apps use it
  • /login, /cart or /api/orders in any web backend.
  • Webhook addresses that receive notifications from payment providers.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/routes/quiz.routes.js registers GET /, POST /, GET /:id and POST /generate, mounted under /api/quizzes in server/src/app.js.

Controller

Definition

In one sentence: The function that handles one route: it reads the request, checks it, asks the right service to do the work, and sends the response.

In more detail: Controllers deal with the web side of things (URL parameters, request bodies, status codes) and leave the actual business rules to services. That keeps each layer focused: controllers don't talk to the database, and services don't know about HTTP.

Real-life example

A waiter: takes your order, checks it's on the menu, passes it to the kitchen, and brings back the plate (or explains what went wrong).

Where real apps use it
  • Web frameworks such as Rails, Laravel and Spring are built around controllers.
  • Most REST APIs organise their handlers this way.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/controllers/quiz.controller.js → createQuiz checks the body with quizSchema, calls quizService.createQuiz, and replies 201 or 400.

Service layer

Definition

In one sentence: The part of the backend that holds the real business rules and data access, kept separate from how requests arrive.

In more detail: Services are plain functions (or classes) that do the actual work, such as saving a quiz or scoring an answer, and can be used from several entry points: REST controllers, socket handlers or scripts. Because they know nothing about HTTP, they are easier to reuse and to test.

Real-life example

The kitchen: it cooks the same dish whether the order came from a waiter, a phone call or a delivery app.

Where real apps use it
  • A payment service used by both a shop's website and its phone app.
  • An email service called from sign-up, password reset and receipts.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/services/quiz.service.js → getQuizById is used by both the REST controller (getQuiz) and the socket handler for host:create-room.

Validation

Definition

In one sentence: Checking that incoming data has the right shape and stays within the allowed limits before using it.

In more detail: Validation catches missing fields, wrong types, text that is too long or numbers out of range, and rejects them with a clear error. It must happen on the server, because anyone can skip the checks in a browser. Validating early keeps bad data out of the database and the game.

Real-life example

A clerk at the passport office who sends back forms with missing signatures before they go any further.

Where real apps use it
  • Sign-up forms checking that an email address looks valid.
  • Payment APIs rejecting negative amounts.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/controllers/quiz.controller.js → createQuiz runs quizSchema.safeParse(req.body); server/src/services/room.service.js → addPlayer checks the nickname's length and uniqueness.

Schema

Definition

In one sentence: A written description of what valid data looks like: which fields exist, what type each one is, and what limits apply.

In more detail: A schema can describe a database table (its columns and types), a JSON document (JSON Schema), or validation rules in code (a Zod schema). Code then checks real data against it. Using one schema in several places keeps the rules the same everywhere.

Real-life example

A cookie cutter: dough that fits the shape is accepted, everything else is trimmed off or rejected.

Where real apps use it
  • Database table definitions.
  • API documentation formats such as OpenAPI.
  • Form validation in web apps.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/validation/quiz.schema.js → questionSchema checks both host-written quizzes and AI output (server/src/services/ai.service.js → generatedSchema); the Postgres tables have their own schema (section 7).

Allowlist vs denylist

Definition

In one sentence: An allowlist names exactly what is permitted and blocks everything else; a denylist names what is forbidden and allows everything else.

In more detail: Allowlists are safer, because anything you forgot to think about is blocked by default; with a denylist, anything you forgot gets through. They are used for allowed values in a field, allowed fields to copy into a response, and allowed websites.

Real-life example

The guest list at a private party (allowlist) versus a list of banned people at a public bar (denylist).

Where real apps use it
  • CORS settings naming the websites allowed to call an API.
  • Phone app permissions you grant one by one.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/validation/ai.schema.js → difficulty: z.enum(["easy", "medium", "hard"]); server/src/services/question.service.js → getPublicQuestion copies only text and options; CLIENT_URL is a one-website allowlist.

Rate limiting

Definition

In one sentence: Limiting how many times someone can do something within a period of time.

In more detail: The server counts requests per user (or per IP address) and rejects the extra ones with 429 "Too Many Requests", often saying when to try again. It protects expensive or easily abused actions (AI calls, login attempts, sending messages) from overuse and attacks.

Real-life example

A fairground ride with a limit of ten rides per wristband per hour.

Where real apps use it
  • Login pages limiting wrong password attempts.
  • Public APIs with request quotas.
  • Messaging apps limiting how many chats you can forward a message to.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/middlewares/aiRateLimit.js allows 10 AI generations per user per hour, but it is never reached because of the duplicate route (section 14, issue 2).

Sliding window

Definition

In one sentence: A way of counting requests over "the last hour from right now", a window that keeps moving forward, instead of per fixed clock hour.

In more detail: With a fixed window (say 14:00 to 15:00), someone could make 10 requests at 14:59 and another 10 at 15:00. A sliding window always looks back exactly one hour from each new request, so bursts around the boundary aren't possible. A simple version stores the time of each request and throws away the old ones.

Real-life example
