A library rule of "at most 5 books in any 7-day period" rather than "5 books per calendar week".

Where real apps use it
  • API rate limits.
  • Fraud checks such as "at most 3 failed card payments in any 10 minutes".
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/middlewares/aiRateLimit.js keeps each user's request times and drops those older than WINDOW_MS (one hour).

Transient error

Definition

In one sentence: A temporary failure that will probably work if you simply try again a little later.

In more detail: Typical causes are a service being briefly overloaded (HTTP 503), a short-term usage limit (429), or a network glitch. These are worth retrying. Permanent errors, such as invalid input (400), are not: retrying just fails again.

Real-life example

A busy phone line: try again in a minute and you'll probably get through.

Where real apps use it
  • Cloud services automatically retrying failed requests.
  • App stores retrying an interrupted download.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/services/ai.service.js → TRANSIENT_STATUSES = [429, 500, 503]; callWithRetry retries only these.

Exponential backoff

Definition

In one sentence: Waiting longer and longer between retries, for example 1 second, then 2, then 4.

In more detail: Doubling the wait gives an overloaded service time to recover instead of flooding it with retries, and a maximum number of attempts stops it going on forever. Many systems also add a little randomness ("jitter") so that many clients don't all retry at the same moment.

Real-life example

Knocking on a door, and waiting a bit longer each time before knocking again.

Where real apps use it
  • Email servers retrying a failed delivery.
  • Phone apps reconnecting after losing signal.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/services/ai.service.js → callWithRetry waits 1000 * 2 ** attempt milliseconds (1 s, then 2 s) for up to 2 retries.

Race condition

Definition

In one sentence: A bug that happens when the result depends on which of two overlapping actions finishes first.

In more detail: When two actions overlap (two clicks, two browser tabs, a reply arriving after the user has left), each one may assume nothing changed in between. In Node.js this happens around await, because other events run while a function is waiting. The fix is to check again after waiting, or to block the second action with a flag or a database transaction.

Real-life example

Two people booking the last seat on a plane at the same moment, each seeing "1 seat available".

Where real apps use it
  • Double payments when a "Pay" button is clicked twice.
  • Two people editing the same record and one silently overwriting the other.
Where in QUIZZY

The host:create-room handler in server/src/sockets/socket.js sets socket.data.creatingRoom, then checks findRoomByHost and socket.connected again after awaiting getQuizById.

In-memory state

Definition

In one sentence: Data a server keeps in its own working memory (RAM) instead of in a database.

In more detail: It is very fast and simple (just JavaScript objects), but it disappears when the server restarts and isn't shared between several copies of the server. It suits short-lived data such as a live game.

Real-life example

Keeping the score on a whiteboard in the room rather than in the filing cabinet.

Where real apps use it
  • Game servers holding the state of a live match.
  • Caches that keep recent results close at hand.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/services/room.service.js → the rooms Map holds every live game; results are only written to the database at the end, by server/src/services/session.service.js.

Grace period

Definition

In one sentence: A short wait before taking an action that can't be undone, giving someone the chance to come back first.

In more detail: Instead of reacting immediately to something like a disconnect, the system starts a timer; if the person returns before it runs out, the timer is cancelled and nothing happens.

Real-life example

A car park that gives you ten minutes after paying to drive out.

Where real apps use it
  • Subscription services keeping your account active for a few days after a failed payment.
  • Chat apps waiting a little before showing someone as offline.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/sockets/socket.js → HOST_GRACE_MS (60 seconds): when the host disconnects a timer starts, and host:resume cancels it.

Load balancer and sticky sessions

Definition

In one sentence: A load balancer spreads users across several copies of a server; sticky sessions make sure the same user keeps going to the same copy.

In more detail: When one server isn't enough, you run several copies behind a load balancer. Connections that hold state, like Socket.IO's long-polling, need every request from one browser to reach the same copy, hence sticky sessions. A shared store such as Redis then lets the copies share data.

Real-life example

A supermarket manager sending each customer to a free checkout; once you have started unloading your shopping, you stay at that checkout until you are done.

Where real apps use it
  • Every large website runs many server copies behind load balancers.
  • Real-time apps using sticky sessions so long-polling connections work.
Where in QUIZZY

Not used: QUIZZY runs one server instance on Render. It is part of the scaling plan in sections 12 and 13.

Redis

Definition

In one sentence: A very fast database that keeps its data in memory, often used as a shared scratchpad between several servers.

In more detail: Redis stores keys with values (text, lists, counters and more) and can delete keys automatically after a set time. Because it is fast and shared, it is commonly used for caches, rate limits, sessions and passing real-time messages between server copies; Socket.IO has a Redis adapter for exactly that.

Real-life example

A shared whiteboard in the staff room that every shift can read and update.

Where real apps use it
  • Caching pages and query results.
  • Game leaderboards.
  • Rate limiting across many servers.
Where in QUIZZY

Not used today. Sections 12 and 13 suggest it for holding rooms and rate-limit counters so QUIZZY could run on several servers.

Health check route

Definition

In one sentence: A tiny web address a server answers just to show that it is alive.

In more detail: Hosting platforms and monitoring tools call it regularly; if it stops answering, they can alert someone or restart the server. It should be quick and need no login.

Real-life example

A nurse checking a patient's pulse.

Where real apps use it
  • Cloud platforms checking /health before sending traffic to a server.
  • Uptime monitors that alert you when a site goes down.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/app.js → GET / replies "QUIZZY Server is running!"; calling it is also a way to wake the sleeping free Render server.

3.6 Databases

Database

Definition

In one sentence: An organised, permanent store of data that programs can search and update safely.

In more detail: A database keeps data on disk so it survives restarts, lets many users read and write at the same time without corrupting anything, and answers questions about the data ("queries") quickly. The database management system, such as PostgreSQL, is the program that does all of this.

Real-life example

A well-organised library with a librarian who fetches and files books for you.

Where real apps use it
  • User accounts on every website.
  • Product catalogues in online shops.
  • Bank account records.
Where in QUIZZY

Supabase's Postgres database stores quizzes, questions, sessions and results; server/src/db/supaBase.js connects to it.

Relational database

Definition

In one sentence: A database that stores data in tables and links the tables together through shared ID numbers.

In more detail: Each kind of thing gets its own table, and relationships are stored with keys: a question row stores the ID of its quiz. SQL queries can combine tables. Relational databases enforce rules (types, unique keys, foreign keys) and support transactions. PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite are examples.

Real-life example

A set of spreadsheets that refer to each other by ID numbers, with a strict clerk who refuses entries that break the rules.

Where real apps use it
  • Banking systems.
  • Online shop orders and stock.
  • School and hospital records.
Where in QUIZZY

QUIZZY's four tables (quizzes, questions, sessions, results) are linked by quiz_id and session_id (section 7.2).

Table, row and column

Definition

In one sentence: A table holds one kind of thing, each row is one item, and each column is one property that every item has.

In more detail: It works like a spreadsheet: the questions table has one row per question and columns such as text, options and correct_index. Every column has a type (text, whole number, UUID and so on), and every row has the same columns.

Real-life example

A class register: one row per student, with columns for name, date of birth and so on.

Where real apps use it
  • A users table in almost every app.
  • An orders table in an online shop.
Where in QUIZZY

The questions table has one row per question with the columns id, quiz_id, position, text, options and correct_index (section 7.2).

SQL

Definition

In one sentence: The language used to ask a relational database for data or to change the data in it.

In more detail: SQL (Structured Query Language) statements such as SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE describe what you want, and the database works out how to do it. Libraries like supabase-js write these requests for you.

Real-life example

A standard request slip at a library: you write down what you want, and the librarian finds it.

Where real apps use it
  • Every relational database.
  • Data analysts writing reports.
Where in QUIZZY

QUIZZY's server writes no raw SQL: server/src/services/quiz.service.js uses supabase-js (from(…).select(…)), and the SQL lives inside the create_quiz and save_session_results database functions.

Primary key

Definition

In one sentence: A column whose value uniquely identifies each row in a table.

In more detail: No two rows can share a primary key, and it can never be empty. Other tables use it to refer to that row. QUIZZY uses UUIDs as primary keys, and the database automatically builds an index on primary keys so lookups by ID are fast.

Real-life example

A student ID number: names can repeat, ID numbers never do.

Where real apps use it
  • User IDs.
  • Order numbers.
Where in QUIZZY

quizzes.id, questions.id, sessions.id and results.id are UUID primary keys; server/src/services/quiz.service.js → getQuizById finds a quiz with .eq("id", id).

Foreign key

Definition

In one sentence: A column that stores another table's primary key to link two rows, and the database refuses links to rows that don't exist.

In more detail: questions.quiz_id must contain an existing quizzes.id. This guarantee ("referential integrity") prevents orphaned data, such as a question belonging to no quiz. Foreign keys also tell tools like Supabase how tables relate, which makes combined queries possible.

Real-life example

A library loan slip that must contain a real member number; the system won't accept a made-up one.

Where real apps use it
  • Orders pointing to customers.
  • Comments pointing to posts.
Where in QUIZZY

questions.quiz_id → quizzes.id, sessions.quiz_id → quizzes.id, results.session_id → sessions.id; server/src/services/quiz.service.js → getQuizById relies on the first to load a quiz together with its questions.

One-to-many relationship

Definition

In one sentence: A link between tables where one row in the first table connects to many rows in the second.

In more detail: It is stored with a foreign key on the "many" side: each question has one quiz_id, and one quiz can have many questions. Other kinds are one-to-one, and many-to-many (which needs an extra linking table).

Real-life example

A parent and children: each child has one birth mother, but a mother can have many children.

Where real apps use it
  • One customer with many orders.
  • One post with many comments.
Where in QUIZZY

quizzes → questions and sessions → results (figure 7.2).

JOIN

Definition

In one sentence: Combining rows from two tables into one result by matching them on a shared column.

In more detail: A SQL JOIN lines up, for example, each quiz with its questions where questions.quiz_id = quizzes.id. Supabase hides the JOIN behind "embedded" selects: asking for questions(…) inside a quizzes query makes it join along the foreign key for you.

Real-life example

Stapling each order slip to the matching customer's card.

Where real apps use it
  • Showing posts together with their authors' names.
  • Showing an order together with its products.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/services/quiz.service.js → getQuizById selects "id, title, creator_id, questions(id, position, text, options, correct_index)" in one query; listQuizzes uses questions(count).

Index (database)

Definition

In one sentence: An extra lookup structure the database keeps so it can find rows quickly without reading the whole table.

In more detail: Like the index at the back of a book, it is sorted by one or more columns and points to the matching rows. It makes searching and sorting fast, but uses extra space and makes writing slightly slower. Postgres automatically indexes primary keys; foreign keys and other columns only get an index if you create one.

Real-life example

The index at the back of a textbook: look up "photosynthesis" and jump straight to page 212.

Where real apps use it
  • Finding a user by email address at login.
  • Sorting orders by date.
Where in QUIZZY

QUIZZY's primary keys are indexed automatically. Useful extra indexes would be questions(quiz_id, position) and quizzes(creator_id, created_at); whether they exist isn't visible in the dashboard (section 7.7).

UUID

Definition

In one sentence: A long random ID, like 1c0ba4c7-a2c3-4c7f-…, that is practically guaranteed to be unique without anyone keeping count.

In more detail: A UUID (Universally Unique Identifier) is 128 bits written as 32 hexadecimal characters in five groups. Random (version 4) UUIDs can be created anywhere (browser, server, database) with a negligible chance of two ever being the same, and unlike 1, 2, 3 they can't be guessed.

Real-life example

A lottery ticket number with so many digits that two tickets never match.

Where real apps use it
  • Database IDs in many systems.
  • Identifiers for files, devices and orders.
Where in QUIZZY

All four tables use UUID primary keys; server/src/services/quiz.service.js → isValidId checks that an ID looks like a UUID; client/src/pages/CreateQuizPage.jsx uses crypto.randomUUID() for temporary React keys.

Transaction

Definition

In one sentence: A group of database changes that is saved as one unit, so either all of the changes happen or none of them do.

In more detail: If any step inside a transaction fails, the database "rolls back", meaning it undoes the earlier steps, so you never get half-finished data. Postgres transactions follow the ACID guarantees. In Postgres, a single database-function call automatically runs inside one transaction, which is why QUIZZY puts saves that touch two tables into functions.

Real-life example

A bank transfer: money leaving account A and arriving in account B is one action, and if the deposit fails, the withdrawal is cancelled, so money never disappears halfway.

Where real apps use it
  • Banking and payment apps moving money.
  • Online shops creating an order and reducing the stock together.
  • Ticket booking, reserving a seat and recording the booking so two people can't get the same seat.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/services/quiz.service.js → createQuiz calls the create_quiz database function, which saves the quiz and all its questions in one transaction; server/src/services/session.service.js → saveSessionResults does the same for sessions and results.

ACID

Definition

In one sentence: Four promises a database makes about transactions: all-or-nothing, the rules are always kept, other users don't disturb you, and saved means saved.

In more detail: Atomicity: all steps or none. Consistency: the data always obeys the rules (types, keys). Isolation: transactions running at the same time don't see each other's half-finished work. Durability: once saved ("committed"), the data survives crashes. PostgreSQL provides all four.

Real-life example

A bank transfer that happens completely (atomic), follows the bank's rules (consistent), can't see other customers' half-done transfers (isolated), and is recorded permanently in the ledger (durable).

Where real apps use it
  • Banking and payment systems.
  • Booking and stock systems that must never double-sell.
Where in QUIZZY

create_quiz and save_session_results each run as one Postgres transaction (called from server/src/services/quiz.service.js → createQuiz and server/src/services/session.service.js → saveSessionResults).

Migration (database)

Definition

In one sentence: A saved script, kept with the code, that changes the database structure one step at a time.

In more detail: Instead of clicking changes in a dashboard, each change (create a table, add a column) is written as a numbered SQL file. Running the migrations in order rebuilds the exact same database anywhere, and code review shows every change. Tools such as the Supabase CLI manage them.

Real-life example

Building plans filed with the council: anyone can rebuild the same house from the plans, step by step.

Where real apps use it
  • Web frameworks such as Rails and Django, which have migrations built in.
  • Teams keeping their test and live databases identical.
Where in QUIZZY

QUIZZY has no migrations: the tables and functions were created in the Supabase dashboard. Adding them is a recommended improvement (sections 12 and 14).

Row Level Security (RLS)

Definition

In one sentence: A database feature that decides, row by row, which rows each user is allowed to see or change.

In more detail: When RLS is switched on for a table, every query from a normal (non-admin) user is filtered by rules called policies, such as "only rows where creator_id is the logged-in user". With RLS on and no policies, normal users can't access the table at all. Admin keys, such as Supabase's secret key, bypass RLS.

Real-life example

A hotel key card that only opens your own room, even though every room is in the same building.

Where real apps use it
  • Apps where the browser talks to the database directly, such as many apps built on Supabase.
  • Business software keeping each company's data separate in one database.
Where in QUIZZY

QUIZZY's browser never queries tables, and the dashboard suggests RLS is on with no policies (section 7.6), so the public key opens nothing; server/src/db/supaBase.js uses the secret key, which bypasses RLS.

Database function (RPC)

Definition

In one sentence: A small program stored inside the database that the app can call by name over the network.

In more detail: A Postgres function contains SQL (and logic such as variables and loops) and runs entirely inside the database, as one transaction. RPC means "Remote Procedure Call": calling a function that lives somewhere else as if it were local. Supabase makes such functions callable with supabase.rpc("name", args).

Real-life example

A vending machine's "meal deal" button: one press, several items, all handled inside the machine.

Where real apps use it
  • Saving data that spans several tables in one step.
  • Reports calculated inside the database, close to the data.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/services/quiz.service.js → createQuiz calls supabase.rpc("create_quiz", …); server/src/services/session.service.js → saveSessionResults calls supabase.rpc("save_session_results", …).

Cascade delete

Definition

In one sentence: A database rule that automatically deletes the child rows when their parent row is deleted.

In more detail: It is set on a foreign key with ON DELETE CASCADE: deleting a quiz would then also delete its questions, instead of the database refusing the delete (the default) or leaving orphans behind. It is powerful but dangerous, because one delete can remove a lot of data.

Real-life example

Deleting a folder on your computer, which also deletes every file inside it.

Where real apps use it
  • Deleting an account also deleting that account's posts.
  • Deleting a project also deleting its tasks.
Where in QUIZZY

QUIZZY has no delete feature yet, and whether its foreign keys cascade isn't visible in the dashboard. If deleting quizzes is added, the questions should cascade, and someone has to decide what happens to old sessions and results.

snake_case vs camelCase

Definition

In one sentence: Two styles of writing names: snake_case joins words with underscores (correct_index), camelCase joins them with capital letters (correctIndex).

In more detail: SQL databases usually use snake_case, while JavaScript uses camelCase. Code that moves data between the two converts the names in one place, so the rest of the code only ever sees one style.

Real-life example

Translating a form at the border, so people on each side read it in their own language.

Where real apps use it
  • Most backends converting database rows into program objects.
  • API libraries that convert field names automatically.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/services/quiz.service.js → toQuiz converts creator_id → creatorId and correct_index → correctIndex; the JSON sent to create_quiz still uses correctIndex (section 7.2).

3.7 Security and authentication

Authentication

Definition

In one sentence: Checking who you are.

In more detail: Usually done with something you know (a password), something you have (a code sent to your phone) or something you are (a fingerprint). Once you are authenticated, the app gives you a session or token so you don't have to prove it again on every click.

Real-life example

Showing your ID card at a building's reception desk.

Where real apps use it
  • Logging in to your email.
  • Unlocking a banking app with your face or fingerprint.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/pages/LoginPage.jsx → handleSubmit calls supabase.auth.signInWithPassword; the server then checks the resulting token in server/src/middlewares/requireAuth.js and server/src/sockets/socketAuth.js.

Authorization

Definition

In one sentence: Checking what you are allowed to do, once we know who you are.

In more detail: Authorization rules look like "only the quiz's owner may host it". They are checked on the server, after authentication, and for every single action, not just once at login.

Real-life example

Your ID gets you into the building (authentication); your key card decides which rooms you can open (authorization).

Where real apps use it
  • Only admins can delete other users' accounts.
  • You can edit your own posts but not other people's.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/controllers/quiz.controller.js → getQuiz checks quiz.creatorId !== req.user.id; server/src/services/room.service.js → startQuiz checks room.hostId. Section 8.5 lists every rule.

Password hashing

Definition

In one sentence: Storing a scrambled "fingerprint" of a password instead of the password itself, so even the people running the database can't read it.

In more detail: A hash function turns the password into a fixed-length string that can't be turned back into the password. At login, the typed password is hashed again and the two hashes are compared. Good password hashes are deliberately slow and add a random value (a "salt") to every password, so stolen hashes are very hard to crack.

Real-life example

A fingerprint: it can confirm that it's you, but nobody can rebuild you from it.

Where real apps use it
  • Every reputable login system.
  • Password managers protecting their own master password.
Where in QUIZZY

QUIZZY's server never sees passwords: Supabase Auth hashes and stores them, and client/src/pages/LoginPage.jsx sends the password straight to Supabase over HTTPS.

Session

Definition

In one sentence: The period during which you stay logged in, and the information the app keeps so it remembers that you are.

In more detail: After login, the app stores something (a cookie or tokens) so you don't have to type your password on every page. In Supabase, a session is an access token plus a refresh token, saved in the browser's localStorage and renewed automatically until you log out. (In QUIZZY's database, the table named sessions means something else: one finished game.)

Real-life example

A day pass at a museum: you show it at each room instead of buying a new ticket every time.

Where real apps use it
  • Staying logged in to a social media site.
  • Shopping sites remembering who you are while you browse.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/auth/AuthContext.jsx → AuthProvider reads the session with supabase.auth.getSession() and keeps it up to date with onAuthStateChange.

Access token

Definition

In one sentence: A short-lived pass the app sends with each request to prove the user is logged in.

In more detail: In QUIZZY it is a JWT that expires after about an hour (Supabase's default). A short lifetime limits the damage if it is ever stolen. The server checks it on every request.

Real-life example

A day ticket: valid today only, and useless tomorrow.

Where real apps use it
  • The APIs of most modern apps.
  • "Log in with Google", which gives the app an access token.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/api.js → apiFetch reads data.session.access_token and sends it; server/src/middlewares/requireAuth.js checks it.

Refresh token

Definition

In one sentence: A longer-lived secret used only to get a new access token when the old one expires, so the user stays logged in.

In more detail: It is sent only to the login service, never with normal requests, and Supabase swaps it for a fresh access token automatically in the background. Logging out cancels it.

Real-life example

Your membership card, which you show at the front desk to get a new day ticket each day.

Where real apps use it
  • Phone apps that keep you logged in for weeks.
  • Big sign-in providers such as Google and Microsoft.
Where in QUIZZY

supabase-js in the browser (client/src/supabase/supabaseClient.js) refreshes tokens automatically; QUIZZY's own code never touches the refresh token.

JWT (JSON Web Token)

Definition

In one sentence: A small digital pass that proves who you are, which the server can check without asking for your password again.

In more detail: It has three parts separated by dots: header, payload and signature. The payload holds facts such as your user ID and the expiry time, and anyone can read it. The signature is made with a secret that only the issuer (Supabase) has, so if anyone changes the payload, the signature no longer matches and the token is rejected.

Real-life example

A concert wristband with a tamper-proof seal: anyone can read the name on it, but you can't change the name without breaking the seal.

Where the analogy breaks down: Unlike a wristband, a JWT also expires after about an hour.

Where real apps use it
  • Logins in many web and phone apps.
  • Single sign-on, where one login works across several apps.
  • APIs that need to know which user is calling.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/api.js → apiFetch sends it in the Authorization header; server/src/middlewares/requireAuth.js verifies it.

Why QUIZZY uses JWTs: they are how the server learns which host is calling without keeping its own list of logged-in users. QUIZZY checks each token by calling supabase.auth.getUser(token) (a network call to Supabase) instead of checking the signature locally. That is simpler and also catches users who have been signed out or deleted, at the cost of one extra network request.

Signature (digital)

Definition

In one sentence: A code attached to data that proves who created it and that it hasn't been changed since.

In more detail: The issuer calculates the signature from the data and a secret key. Anyone verifying it can check that the two still fit together; if even one character of the data changed, they no longer match. A signature doesn't hide the data; it only protects against changes and forgeries.

Real-life example

A wax seal on a letter: anyone can read the letter, but a broken or fake seal shows that someone tampered with it.

Where real apps use it
  • JWTs used for logins.
  • Software updates signed by the company that made them.
  • HTTPS certificates.
Where in QUIZZY

The signature on Supabase's JWTs is what makes the user ID inside them trustworthy; server/src/middlewares/requireAuth.js leaves the actual check to supabase.auth.getUser instead of verifying it itself.

Bearer token

Definition

In one sentence: A token that gives access to whoever presents it (the "bearer"), with no extra proof needed.

In more detail: It is sent in the header Authorization: Bearer <token>. Because simply having it is enough, a bearer token must only travel over HTTPS and must never be logged or shared.

Real-life example

Cash or a cinema ticket: whoever holds it can use it.

Where real apps use it
  • Most REST APIs, including those of GitHub and Google.
  • Phone apps calling their own backends.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/api.js → apiFetch sets Authorization: Bearer ${token}; server/src/middlewares/requireAuth.js splits the header and rejects anything that isn't Bearer <token>.

Secret key vs publishable key

Definition

In one sentence: A publishable key is safe to put in a website and gives only limited access; a secret key gives full admin access and must stay on the server.

In more detail: Supabase's publishable key identifies the project for public actions such as logging in, and its access to tables is limited by Row Level Security. The secret key bypasses RLS completely. Anything in client code can be read by anyone, so secret keys belong only in server environment variables. (Older Supabase projects call them the "anon" key and the "service_role" key.)

Real-life example

A shop's public phone number versus the key to its safe.

Where real apps use it
  • Payment providers: a publishable key in the checkout page, a secret key on the server.
  • Map services, whose public keys are restricted to the company's own website.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/supabase/supabaseClient.js uses VITE_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY; server/src/db/supaBase.js uses SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY.

XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)

Definition

In one sentence: An attack where someone sneaks their own JavaScript into a web page, so it runs in other people's browsers.

In more detail: XSS happens when an app shows text typed by a user as HTML, for example a nickname like <img src=x onerror=…>. The injected script could steal tokens or act as the victim. The defence is to always treat user text as text: React does this automatically for anything inserted with { }, unless you use dangerouslySetInnerHTML.

Real-life example

Someone writes "give the visitor the master key" on a sticky note, and a careless assistant reads it out as an order instead of as a message.

Where real apps use it
  • A classic risk in comment sections and chat messages.
  • Profile names and bios shown to other users.
Where in QUIZZY

Nicknames and quiz text are shown with { } in JSX (for example in client/src/components/Lobby.jsx), so React escapes them; QUIZZY never uses dangerouslySetInnerHTML.

SQL injection

Definition

In one sentence: An attack where text typed by a user ends up being treated as part of a database command.

In more detail: If code builds SQL by gluing user input into a string, input like '); DROP TABLE quizzes; -- can change what the command does. The defence is parameterised queries: the input is sent separately as data and is never mixed into the command itself.

Real-life example

A form where someone writes "and also hand me the safe keys" in the name box, and the clerk obeys it.

Where real apps use it
  • A risk for any search box or login form built with raw SQL.
  • One of the most common causes of data breaches in older websites.
Where in QUIZZY

supabase-js and supabase.rpc send values as parameters (server/src/services/quiz.service.js), so quiz titles and nicknames can't change any query.

Mass assignment

Definition

In one sentence: An attack where a request includes extra fields the server didn't expect, such as isAdmin: true, and the server saves them without checking.

In more detail: It happens when code copies a whole request body into a database record. The defence is to accept only known fields (an allowlist), for example a validation schema that drops unknown fields.

Real-life example

A job application where the applicant adds a line "starting salary: one million", and HR files it without reading.

Where real apps use it
  • "Update my profile" endpoints.
  • Sign-up forms that could be tricked into creating admin accounts.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/validation/quiz.schema.js → quizSchema drops unknown fields, so a creatorId sneaked into the body is removed before server/src/controllers/quiz.controller.js → createQuiz uses the data.

Enumeration attack

Definition

In one sentence: Trying many IDs or usernames to find out which ones exist, based on how the app responds.

In more detail: If an app answers "forbidden" for items that exist but are private and "not found" for items that don't exist, an attacker learns which ones are real. Giving the same answer in both cases, and using IDs that can't be guessed, prevents it.

Real-life example

A hotel receptionist who says "that guest doesn't want visitors" instead of "no such guest", which confirms the guest is staying there.

Where real apps use it
  • Login pages saying "wrong email or password" rather than "no account with that email".
  • Code-hosting sites showing "not found" for private projects you can't see.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/controllers/quiz.controller.js → getQuiz returns 404 both for missing quizzes and for other hosts' quizzes, and quiz IDs are random UUIDs.

Prompt injection

Definition

In one sentence: Tricking an AI model with text that contains instructions, so it ignores the app's own instructions.

In more detail: When user text is placed inside a prompt, the model can't reliably tell the app's instructions apart from the user's. Defences: keep user input short and clearly separated, validate the model's output, limit what the output can do, and keep a human review step.

Real-life example

Slipping a note into a pile of letters for an assistant that says "ignore your boss and do what I say".

Where real apps use it
  • Chatbots and AI assistants.
  • AI tools that read emails or web pages, which may contain hidden instructions.
Where in QUIZZY

The topic is inserted into the prompt in server/src/services/ai.service.js → buildPrompt; it is limited to 100 characters, the output must pass Zod, and the host reviews the questions before saving.

Defense in depth

Definition

In one sentence: Using several independent layers of protection, so one failure doesn't expose everything.

In more detail: Each layer assumes the others might fail: validation, authentication, authorization, database rules, network rules. An attacker has to get through all of them.

Real-life example

A castle with a moat, walls, a gate and guards.

Where real apps use it
  • Banks combining passwords, one-time codes and fraud monitoring.
  • Cloud systems combining firewalls with per-user permissions.
Where in QUIZZY

The ownership checks in server/src/controllers/quiz.controller.js, plus Row Level Security on the Supabase tables, plus CORS in server/src/app.js (section 11).

3.8 AI

Large language model (LLM)

Definition

In one sentence: An AI program, trained on huge amounts of text, that writes new text by repeatedly predicting what should come next.

In more detail: A model such as Gemini takes a prompt and produces a response piece by piece (in "tokens"), choosing likely continuations based on patterns learned in training. It is very good at language tasks but can be confidently wrong (this is called "hallucinating"), so its output must be checked.

Real-life example

An extremely well-read autocomplete.

Where the analogy breaks down: Unlike the autocomplete on your phone, it can follow detailed instructions and produce whole structured documents, which is why it can write a full quiz.

Where real apps use it
  • Chat assistants such as Gemini and ChatGPT.
  • Writing and coding helpers.
  • Customer-support chatbots.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/services/ai.service.js → generateQuestions asks Gemini to write the quiz questions.

API key

Definition

In one sentence: A secret string that identifies your app to a paid or limited service, so the service knows who to bill and which limits apply.

In more detail: It is sent with every request to the service (Gemini here). Unlike a user's login token, it represents the app itself, not a person. Anyone who has it can use up your quota or your money, so it must stay on the server.

Real-life example

A company credit card handed to one department: whoever holds it can spend on the company's account.

Where real apps use it
  • Map services shown inside apps.
  • Payment, weather and AI services.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/services/ai.service.js reads process.env.GEMINI_API_KEY and passes it to new GoogleGenAI({ apiKey }); it is set only on Render and in server/.env.

Prompt

Definition

In one sentence: The instructions and input text you send to an AI model.

In more detail: A clear prompt says what to produce, in what format, and which rules to follow (for example "exactly 4 options, exactly one correct"). Improving the prompt is often the cheapest way to get better results, but it never guarantees the rules are followed, so the output still has to be checked.

Real-life example

A detailed brief you give a freelancer before they start work.

Where real apps use it
  • Messages you type to an AI assistant.
  • Hidden instructions behind AI features in apps, such as "summarise this email".
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/services/ai.service.js → buildPrompt builds the prompt from the topic, difficulty and number of questions.

Structured output

Definition

In one sentence: Asking an AI model to answer in a fixed, machine-readable format, such as JSON with specific fields, instead of free text.

In more detail: With Gemini you pass a JSON Schema and responseMimeType: "application/json", and the model's answer is constrained to that shape. It greatly reduces answers that can't be read by the program, but it doesn't guarantee the content is correct, so you still validate it.

Real-life example

Asking someone to fill in a form instead of writing you a letter.

Where real apps use it
  • AI tools pulling the amount and date out of invoices.
  • Chatbots that call other tools with exact, typed inputs.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/services/ai.service.js → generateQuestions passes responseJsonSchema and then checks the result with generatedSchema (Zod).

JSON Schema

Definition

In one sentence: A standard way to describe what a JSON document must look like: its fields, their types, and which ones are required.

In more detail: A JSON Schema is itself written in JSON, for example { type: "object", properties: …, required: [...] }. Tools use it to check data or, as Gemini does, to restrict what a model may generate. Zod schemas play a similar role inside JavaScript code.

Real-life example

The blank template of a form, showing every box and which ones must be filled in.

Where real apps use it
  • API documentation formats such as OpenAPI.
  • Code editors checking configuration files as you type.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/services/ai.service.js → responseJsonSchema describes { questions: [{ text, options, correctIndex }] }.

Model alias vs pinned model

Definition

In one sentence: An alias is a model name that always points to the newest version; a pinned name stays on one exact version.

In more detail: Aliases give you upgrades automatically, but the model's behaviour can change without warning. Pinned versions behave predictably but are eventually retired, so you must update them yourself. Production apps usually pin a version and upgrade on purpose after testing.

Real-life example

Subscribing to "the latest edition" of a textbook versus ordering "the 3rd edition".

Where real apps use it
  • AI services, which offer both "latest" names and dated version names.
  • Software dependencies, which can follow "latest" or an exact version number.
Where in QUIZZY

The model name comes from the GEMINI_MODEL environment variable (server/src/services/ai.service.js); whether it is an alias or pinned depends on the value set on Render, which this guide doesn't show.

3.9 Building and deploying

Build

Definition

In one sentence: Turning the source code you write into the optimised files that are actually shipped and run.

In more detail: For the client, npm run build (which runs vite build) converts JSX into plain JavaScript, bundles the files, removes unused code and minifies everything, writing the result to client/dist. The Node server needs no build step: Render just installs the packages and runs it.

Real-life example

Printing and binding a book from the author's manuscript.

Where real apps use it
  • Almost every modern website has a build step.
  • Phone apps are "built" into installable packages before going to the app stores.
Where in QUIZZY

client/package.json → "build": "vite build"; Vercel runs it on every deployment.

Bundling

Definition

In one sentence: Combining many code files and libraries into a few files that the browser can download efficiently.

In more detail: A bundler starts at the entry file (main.jsx), follows every import, and packs everything needed into one or a few files, so the browser makes a few requests instead of hundreds. Bundlers can also split code into pieces that load only when needed.

Real-life example

Packing everything for a trip into a few suitcases instead of carrying a hundred loose items.

Where real apps use it
  • Almost all large websites ship bundled JavaScript.
  • Browser extensions and desktop apps built with web technology.
Where in QUIZZY

Vite bundles client/src into client/dist/assets/index-….js and .css; the build warns that the main bundle is over 500 kB.

Minification

Definition

In one sentence: Shrinking code by removing spaces, comments and long names, without changing what it does.

In more detail: Minified code is much smaller, so it downloads faster, but it is very hard for people to read. "Source maps" can map it back to the original code for debugging.

Real-life example

Writing a message in shorthand: shorter to send, same meaning.

Where real apps use it
  • The JavaScript and CSS of nearly every live website.
  • JavaScript libraries published in a ".min.js" version.
Where in QUIZZY

vite build (run by npm run build in client/) minifies the client bundle automatically.

Deployment

Definition

In one sentence: Putting a new version of your app onto the computers where real users can use it.

In more detail: Typically: build the code, upload it, start the new version, and switch users over to it. Platforms like Vercel and Render do all of this automatically. Deploying a server restarts it, which matters when important data lives only in memory.

Real-life example

Restocking a shop's shelves with the new product line overnight.

Where real apps use it
  • Websites that update several times a day.
  • Phone app updates appearing in the app store.
Where in QUIZZY

Pushing to GitHub triggers a Vercel deployment (client) and a Render deployment (server); a Render deployment wipes QUIZZY's in-memory rooms.

Hosting

Definition

In one sentence: Renting space on computers that are always online, so your app can be reached on the internet.

In more detail: A host provides the machines (or a managed platform), the network, HTTPS certificates and domain names. Different hosts suit different kinds of programs: static files, serverless functions, long-running servers or databases.

Real-life example

Renting a shop on a busy street instead of building one yourself.

Where real apps use it
  • Websites hosted on platforms such as Vercel or Netlify.
  • Servers and databases hosted on cloud platforms.
Where in QUIZZY

The client is hosted on Vercel, the server on Render, and the database on Supabase (section 2).

Static site

Definition

In one sentence: A website made of ready-made files that are sent to every visitor exactly as they are, without the server running any code for each request.

In more detail: The HTML, CSS, JavaScript and images are produced once, at build time. Static files are cheap, fast and easy to copy onto a CDN. The site can still be interactive in the browser: a React single-page application is a static site whose JavaScript then calls APIs.

Real-life example

Printed flyers: every visitor gets the same copy.

Where real apps use it
  • Portfolios and documentation websites.
  • The frontends of many single-page applications.
Where in QUIZZY

The built client (client/dist) is a static site served by Vercel; all the dynamic work happens on Render.

Serverless function

Definition

In one sentence: A small piece of server code that a platform starts only when a request arrives, and stops again soon after.

In more detail: You don't manage a server: the platform runs your function for one request (or a short burst), then freezes or discards it. Nothing is kept in memory between requests, and several copies can run at once without sharing memory. It is cheap and scales automatically, but doesn't suit long-lived connections or data held in memory.

Real-life example

A taxi: perfect for one trip, then it's gone.

Where the analogy breaks down: Several taxis can serve you at once, but none of them remembers your previous trip; that lack of memory is exactly why QUIZZY's server can't be serverless.

Where real apps use it
  • Contact forms and webhooks on websites.
  • Image resizing triggered by an upload.
Where in QUIZZY

QUIZZY doesn't use serverless functions: the live game needs a long-running process that holds sockets and the rooms Map (section 10.4).

Long-running process

Definition

In one sentence: A program that starts once and keeps running continuously, handling many requests over hours or days.

In more detail: It can keep data in memory, hold connections open (like WebSockets) and run timers. The trade-offs: you pay for it even while it's idle, and a restart wipes its memory.

Real-life example

A shopkeeper who stays in the shop all day and remembers the regular customers.

Where real apps use it
  • Game servers and chat servers.
  • Database servers.
Where in QUIZZY

server/server.js runs as one long-running Node process on Render, holding the rooms Map and every socket.

Monorepo

Definition

In one sentence: A single Git repository that contains several projects, such as a frontend and a backend.

In more detail: Keeping related code together means one commit can change both sides, and the history lives in one place. Each project still has its own package.json and packages, and the hosting platforms are told which folder to build (the "root directory").

Real-life example

One filing cabinet with a separate drawer for each department.

Where real apps use it
  • Large companies keeping many projects in one repository.
  • Full-stack starter projects with client/ and server/ folders.
Where in QUIZZY

The QUIZZY repository contains client/ and server/, each with its own package.json; Vercel builds client/ and Render runs server/.

Continuous deployment

Definition

In one sentence: Automatically deploying every change pushed to the main branch, with no manual steps.

In more detail: The hosting platform watches the repository, and each push triggers a build and a deployment. It is often combined with automatic tests that run first (continuous integration, CI), so broken code doesn't reach users.

Real-life example

A newspaper that goes to print automatically as soon as an editor approves a story.

Where real apps use it
  • Most modern web teams.
  • Open-source projects publishing a new version when changes are merged.
Where in QUIZZY

Vercel and Render watch the GitHub repository, so a push to main redeploys both (section 10.5); QUIZZY has no automatic tests yet.

Production vs preview

Definition

In one sentence: Production is the live version that real users see; a preview is a temporary copy of a change, used for testing before it goes live.

In more detail: Vercel creates a preview deployment with its own URL for each branch or pull request, and updates production only from the main branch. Previews may need their own settings: for example, the server's CORS allowlist won't include preview URLs.

Real-life example

A dress rehearsal versus opening night.

Where real apps use it
  • Website teams reviewing every change on a preview link.
  • Beta versions of phone apps given to testers before release.
Where in QUIZZY

The production client is the Vercel deployment whose address is set as CLIENT_URL on Render; a preview URL would be blocked by the CORS check in server/src/app.js.

Cold start (free-tier sleep)

Definition

In one sentence: The delay when a sleeping server has to start up before it can answer the first request.

In more detail: Free hosting plans, such as Render's, stop servers that have had no traffic for a while to save resources. The next visitor waits while the server boots, which can take tens of seconds. For QUIZZY, falling asleep also wipes every in-memory room.

Real-life example

Starting a car on a frosty morning: it takes a while before you can drive off.

Where real apps use it
  • Free-tier hosting of hobby projects.
  • Serverless functions that haven't run for a while.
Where in QUIZZY

The free Render instance running server/server.js sleeps after about 15 minutes without traffic; opening QuizListPage wakes it with GET /api/quizzes.

3.10 The technologies QUIZZY uses

Version numbers come from client/package.json and server/package.json. Socket.IO is defined in 3.2 and JWT in 3.7.

React

Definition

In one sentence: A JavaScript library for building user interfaces out of reusable components.

In more detail: You describe what the screen should look like for the current state, and React updates the real page when the state changes. It compares the new description with the previous one and changes only what is different, which is faster and less error-prone than changing the page by hand. It was created at Facebook (now Meta); QUIZZY uses version 19.

Real-life example

Instead of repainting a whole wall when one tile changes, you give a decorator a picture of how the wall should look, and they replace only the tiles that differ.

Where real apps use it
  • Facebook and Instagram on the web.
  • Countless dashboards and admin panels.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/main.jsx → createRoot(…).render(…) starts React; every page in client/src/pages and component in client/src/components is a React component.

Why QUIZZY uses it: the student screen moves through many stages (join form, lobby, question, result, finished, final rank, session ended), and React makes "show the screen that matches the current state" simple: PlayerPage is a chain of if (finalResult) … if (closedMessage) … if (currentQuestion) … early returns.

Vite

Definition

In one sentence: A tool that runs your frontend while you develop it and packages it for production.

In more detail: During development, npm run dev starts a local server that updates the page instantly when you save a file. For production, npm run build bundles and minifies everything into client/dist. Only environment variables whose names start with VITE_ reach browser code, and their values are fixed into the files at build time.

Real-life example

A print shop: while you write, it shows you instant previews; when you are done, it binds your loose pages into a finished book (the dist folder) for the bookshop (Vercel) to sell.

Where real apps use it
  • Modern React and Vue projects.
  • Many newer web frameworks use Vite under the hood.
Where in QUIZZY

client/vite.config.js loads the react() and tailwindcss() plugins; client/src/config/config.js reads import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL.

Why QUIZZY uses it: fast development, built-in JSX support through @vitejs/plugin-react, the Tailwind plugin, and environment variables through import.meta.env.

Common mistake

Changing a VITE_ variable in the Vercel dashboard and expecting the live site to change. Because the values are baked in at build time, you must redeploy. The repository has a commit literally named chore: trigger Vercel deploy, which is exactly this situation.

React Router

Definition

In one sentence: A library that decides which React page to show for each web address.

In more detail: It provides client-side routing: <Route path="/join/:code"> shows PlayerPage for any URL like /join/123456, useParams() reads URL parameters, useNavigate() changes the page from code, and <Navigate> redirects while drawing. QUIZZY uses version 7 (react-router-dom).

Real-life example

A building directory that tells you which room to go to, without making you leave the building.

Where real apps use it
  • Many React single-page applications.
  • Admin dashboards with many pages.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/main.jsx wraps the app in <BrowserRouter>; client/src/App.jsx declares every route (section 5).

Why QUIZZY uses it: shareable links. The QR code on the projector is simply the URL https://<your-site>/join/123456; React Router reads the room code straight from it.

Tailwind CSS

Definition

In one sentence: A styling toolkit where you style elements by adding small ready-made class names, such as rounded-2xl or bg-white.

In more detail: Instead of writing CSS rules in a separate file, you combine "utility classes" on each element. Version 4 is configured in CSS with an @theme block, where custom design values (colours, fonts) automatically become classes. Prefixes like sm: and lg: apply styles only on wider screens, and motion-reduce: respects reduced motion. Classes you never use aren't shipped.

Real-life example

Dressing from a rack of standard clothing pieces instead of sewing a custom outfit for each person.

Where the analogy breaks down: Two pieces of the same kind clash: if an element has both text-lg and text-2xl, the winner is decided by their order in Tailwind's generated CSS, not by the order you wrote them.

Where real apps use it
  • Many modern React and Next.js projects.
  • Ready-made UI component kits built on Tailwind.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/index.css (@import "tailwindcss", the @theme design values and animations); client/src/components/Button.jsx builds its variants from Tailwind classes.

Why QUIZZY uses it: fast, consistent styling with shared design values such as --color-answer-red, and responsive prefixes for the phone-first student screens and projector-first host screens.

Node.js

Definition

In one sentence: A program that runs JavaScript outside the browser, so JavaScript can power servers.

In more detail: Node.js is a runtime built on the same JavaScript engine as Google Chrome. It handles many connections at once with a single thread and an event loop, and it comes with npm, the largest collection of reusable packages. QUIZZY's server uses the older CommonJS module style (require).

Real-life example

The same language (JavaScript) moving to a new country (the server) and getting a new set of tools there.

Where real apps use it
  • Web servers and APIs at companies of every size.
  • Developer tools such as Vite and the npm command itself.
Where in QUIZZY

server/package.json → "start": "node server.js"; server/server.js is the entry point on Render.

Why QUIZZY uses it: the same language on both sides, an excellent WebSocket library (Socket.IO), and, because there is only one thread, the in-memory rooms Map is never changed by two pieces of code at the same instant: each event handler runs until its next await before another starts.

Express (with cors and dotenv)

Definition

In one sentence: A small Node.js library for building web servers and APIs by declaring routes and middleware.

In more detail: You write app.use(…) for middleware and router.get(…) or router.post(…) for routes. Express 5 automatically passes errors from async handlers to its error handling. Two helper packages go with it in QUIZZY: cors, a middleware that adds the CORS headers, and dotenv, which loads a local .env file into process.env (on Render there is no .env file, so it simply does nothing).

Real-life example

A mail-sorting room: every letter passes the same stations (middleware) before reaching the right desk (route handler).

Where real apps use it
  • Countless Node.js APIs, from small projects to large companies.
  • Backends for single-page and phone apps.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/app.js (cors(…), express.json(), app.use("/api/quizzes", quizRouter)); server/src/routes/quiz.routes.js; server/server.js line 1 calls require("dotenv").config().

Why QUIZZY uses it: a small, well-known way to offer the four quiz endpoints, with requireAuth applied once to the whole router.

Supabase and PostgreSQL

Definition

In one sentence: Supabase is a hosted service that gives you a PostgreSQL database, user logins and a ready-made API, without running any servers yourself.

In more detail: PostgreSQL ("Postgres") is a popular open-source relational database. Supabase runs it for you and adds an authentication service, an automatic REST API for your tables, the @supabase/supabase-js client library (so you write supabase.from("quizzes").select(…) instead of raw SQL), a dashboard, and two kinds of keys.

Real-life example

Postgres is a well-organised filing cabinet; Supabase is the office around it, with a receptionist who fetches files (the API), a security desk issuing ID badges (Auth), and keys deciding who may open which drawer.

Where real apps use it
  • Many startups and side projects build their whole backend on Supabase.
  • PostgreSQL itself is one of the most widely used databases, from small apps to large companies.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/db/supaBase.js (server client with the secret key) and client/src/supabase/supabaseClient.js (browser client with the publishable key); all queries are in server/src/services/quiz.service.js and session.service.js.

Why QUIZZY uses it: one managed service provides both the database and user accounts, with a free tier and no database server to run. QUIZZY uses the publishable key in the browser (login only) and the secret key on the server (all database access); see section 7.

Supabase Auth

Definition

In one sentence: Supabase's ready-made login system: it stores accounts, checks passwords and hands out login tokens.

In more detail: In the browser, supabase.auth.signUp and signInWithPassword create a session (an access token plus a refresh token), which supabase-js stores and renews automatically. On the server, supabase.auth.getUser(token) asks Supabase whether a token is valid and whose it is. Projects can require users to confirm their email before logging in.

Real-life example

The security desk of an office building, which checks your ID once and gives you a badge you show everywhere else.

Where real apps use it
  • Apps built on Supabase.
  • Similar services such as Firebase Authentication and Auth0 do the same job for other apps.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/pages/LoginPage.jsx → handleSubmit; client/src/auth/AuthContext.jsx → AuthProvider; server/src/middlewares/requireAuth.js and server/src/sockets/socketAuth.js call getUser.

Why QUIZZY uses it: hosts need accounts to own quizzes, and building secure password storage and token signing yourself is risky and slow. Students deliberately need no account.

Zod

Definition

In one sentence: A JavaScript library for checking that data has the shape you expect, with clear error messages when it doesn't.

In more detail: You describe valid data once as a schema; schema.safeParse(input) then returns either { success: true, data } with cleaned data or { success: false, error } with readable messages. z.object also drops unknown fields by default, which blocks mass assignment.

Real-life example

An airport baggage sizer: the bag either fits the frame or it doesn't, and you are told exactly which side is too big.

Where real apps use it
  • Checking form input and API requests in many JavaScript and TypeScript projects.
  • Checking configuration and environment variables when an app starts.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/validation/quiz.schema.js (questionSchema, quizSchema), server/src/validation/ai.schema.js (generateRequestSchema), and server/src/services/ai.service.js → generatedSchema.

Why QUIZZY uses it: never trust input. Zod checks the quizzes hosts save, the AI generation requests, and the AI's own output. The same questionSchema is used for human-written and AI-written questions, so both follow identical rules.

Google Gemini (@google/genai)

Definition

In one sentence: Google's family of AI models, which QUIZZY uses to write quiz questions.

In more detail: Gemini models are large language models. The @google/genai library calls them with ai.models.generateContent(…). QUIZZY uses structured output (a JSON Schema plus responseMimeType: "application/json") so the answer arrives in a predictable shape, and picks the model through the GEMINI_MODEL environment variable.

Real-life example

A very well-read assistant who fills in a printed form for you, instead of writing a free-form letter.

Where real apps use it
  • Google's Gemini app and the AI features in Google's products.
  • Developers' own apps, which call the same models through Google's API.
Where in QUIZZY

server/src/services/ai.service.js → generateQuestions, buildPrompt, callWithRetry; called from server/src/controllers/quiz.controller.js → generateQuiz and, in the browser, from client/src/pages/CreateQuizPage.jsx → handleGenerate.

Why QUIZZY uses it: writing quizzes by hand is slow; the host types a topic, difficulty and number of questions, then reviews the generated questions before saving. Because the model name is an environment variable, it can be changed without touching the code.

Vercel

Definition

In one sentence: A hosting platform that builds websites straight from GitHub and serves them quickly all over the world.

In more detail: Vercel runs your build on every push, serves the static result from its CDN, can run serverless functions, and creates preview deployments for branches. Settings such as rewrites live in vercel.json, and environment variables are set in its dashboard.

Real-life example

A chain of vending machines restocked automatically: perfect for handing out pre-packed items instantly, but you can't hold a long conversation with a vending machine.

Where real apps use it
  • Hosting for Next.js sites and many other frontends.
  • Preview links for every pull request in many web teams.
Where in QUIZZY

client/vercel.json sends every path to index.html; Vercel hosts the built client.

Why QUIZZY uses it: free, automatic deployments of the static React build. Only the client is hosted there; section 10 explains why the server is not.

Render

Definition

In one sentence: A hosting platform that keeps your server program running all the time and gives it a public HTTPS address.

In more detail: You connect a repository and give a build command and a start command; Render installs, starts and restarts the program, sets the PORT variable, and redeploys on every push. Free web services sleep after a period without traffic.

Real-life example

Renting a small shop with a permanent shopkeeper (your Node process) who can talk to customers for as long as they like, unlike the vending machine.

Where real apps use it
  • Hosting APIs and background workers for small teams and side projects.
  • Hosting small databases alongside them.
Where in QUIZZY

Runs server/ with npm start (node server.js); server/server.js listens on process.env.PORT.

Why QUIZZY uses it: Socket.IO needs a process that stays running and keeps the connections and the rooms Map in memory.

qrcode.react (QR codes)

Definition

In one sentence: A React component that draws a QR code for any text, right in the browser.

In more detail: A QR code is a square barcode that phone cameras can read; it usually contains a URL. The library works out the pattern of squares and draws it as SVG, so it stays sharp at any size, even on a projector. Its error-correction setting lets the code still scan when part of it is blurred or covered.

Real-life example

A printed address label that a phone camera can read instead of a person.

Where real apps use it
  • Restaurant menus and payment codes.
  • Joining a Wi-Fi network or opening an event ticket.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/pages/HostPage.jsx → <QRCodeSVG value={joinLink} … /> in the host lobby.

motion (animation library)

Definition

In one sentence: An animation library for React that makes elements move smoothly, including sliding into new positions when a list reorders.

In more detail: Writing <motion.li layout> makes an element remember where it was; when its position changes, motion measures the old and new positions and animates the difference. <MotionConfig reducedMotion="user"> switches movement off for users who ask for reduced motion. It is the successor to the library known as Framer Motion.

Real-life example

Runners' names on a race board sliding past each other as positions change, instead of jumping.

Where real apps use it
  • Animated menus and page transitions in React apps.
  • Drag-and-drop lists that reorder smoothly.
Where in QUIZZY

client/src/components/Leaderboard.jsx → motion.li layout for the rows, the podium animation, and MotionConfig.

Why QUIZZY uses these two: students join by scanning the projector instead of typing a URL, and leaderboard rows slide when ranks change, which makes the live board easy to follow from the back of a classroom.

Interview tip

For every technology, interviewers want the reason, not just the definition. Practise one line each: "Socket.IO because the host's screen must react to other people's actions", "Zod because I validate the AI's output too, not just user input", "Render instead of Vercel for the server because WebSockets need a long-running process."

This section lists every file in client/src and server/src (plus the two entry files server/server.js and client/index.html), what each one is responsible for, which local files it imports, and which files import it. The .kilo/worktrees/ folder in the repository is a separate copy of the project made by an editor tool and is ignored here.

Key terms here (defined in section 3): Module (import and export) · npm package (dependency)

4.3 Dependency diagrams

Arrows point from a file to the file it imports. To keep the client diagram readable, the six small presentational components (Button, Card, Input, ErrorMessage, CenteredPage, Spinner) are drawn as one "UI kit" box.

Figure 4.1a: Client import graph, part 1: entry, auth and the three connection helpers (REST, host socket, student socket).
Figure 4.1b: Client import graph, part 2: pages and their components.
Figure 4.2: Server import graph. Rounded boxes are npm packages.
Key idea

Only four server files touch the database (requireAuth, socketAuth, quiz.service, session.service), and only one file (room.service.js) owns the live game state. If you know those five files, you know where every piece of data lives.

Common mistake

Missing or mismatched exports. quiz.routes.js still contains console.log("controller exports:", Object.keys(quizController)), a leftover from debugging exactly this: if a controller function is not listed in module.exports, router.get("/", quizController.listQuizzes) receives undefined and Express crashes on startup. On the client, mixing up default and named imports (import apiFetch from "../api" instead of import { apiFetch } from "../api") gives undefined at run time. Also remember to save the file: an unsaved editor tab is not what Vite or nodemon runs.

5.1 How a page decides what to show

Neither HostPage nor PlayerPage uses sub-routes for their stages. Instead they return different JSX depending on state, checked in a fixed order. This is a simple state machine:

Figure 5.1: The student screen (PlayerPage). The order of the if checks is finalResult → closedMessage → finished → currentQuestion → joined → join form.
Figure 5.2: The host screen (HostPage). Order of checks: checking → no roomCode → leaderboard → lobby.
Key idea

The URL only says which quiz or room; the socket events decide which stage of the game is on screen. That is why refreshing /host/:quizId works: the page reconnects, asks the server "do I have a room?" (host:resume) and rebuilds its state from the answer.

Common mistake

Forgetting client/vercel.json. Without its rewrite rule, opening /join/123456 directly (which is exactly what a QR scan does) asks Vercel for a file called /join/123456, which doesn't exist, and returns a 404. The rewrite serves index.html for every path so React Router can handle it.

Interview tip

If asked "how do you protect routes in React?", explain that RequireAuth is only a user-experience guard: it hides pages from logged-out users. The real protection is on the server (requireAuth and socketAuth), because anyone can change JavaScript running in their own browser.

6.How the frontend talks to the backend

The client talks to the server in two ways. REST over HTTPS is used for things that happen once and return an answer: list quizzes, save a quiz, generate questions with AI. Socket.IO over WSS is used for the live game, where the server must push updates the moment other people act.

Key idea

Use request/response (REST) when the user asks for something. Use a persistent socket when the server needs to tell you something you didn't ask for, like "a student just joined" or "Ana just answered question 4".

6.1 REST: apiFetch and the Authorization header

Every REST call from the client goes through one small helper, so the token and base URL are never forgotten:

client/src/api.js → apiFetch
export const apiFetch = async (path, options = {}) => {
  const { data } = await supabase.auth.getSession();
  const token = data.session?.access_token;

  return fetch(`${API_URL}${path}`, {
    ...options,
    headers: {
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
      ...options.headers,
      ...(token ? { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } : {}),
    },
  });
};
  • API_URL comes from client/src/config/config.js (VITE_API_URL), e.g. the Render address.
  • supabase.auth.getSession() is called on every request. supabase-js refreshes the access token automatically when it is about to expire, so each request carries a fresh token.
  • The token goes in the standard header Authorization: Bearer <JWT>. "Bearer" means "whoever bears (holds) this token is the user".
  • apiFetch returns the raw Response; the pages call res.json() and check res.ok themselves (e.g. CreateQuizPage → handleSubmit).

6.2 CORS and CLIENT_URL

Key terms here (defined in section 3): Origin · CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) · Preflight request · Request header

In production, the page comes from Vercel and the API is on Render: two different origins. So the server must allow the Vercel origin, and it does so in two places, both read from the CLIENT_URL environment variable:

server/src/app.js and server/server.js
// Express (REST)
app.use(cors({ origin: process.env.CLIENT_URL || "http://localhost:5173" }));

// Socket.IO (its first requests are HTTP long-polling, which CORS also governs)
const io = new Server(httpServer, { cors: { origin: CLIENT_URL } });
Common mistake
  • Trailing slash or wrong scheme: CLIENT_URL=https://quizzy.vercel.app/ does not match the origin https://quizzy.vercel.app, so every request fails with a CORS error in the browser console.
  • Localhost fallback in production: if CLIENT_URL is not set on Render, both lines fall back to http://localhost:5173, and the deployed site is blocked. The same happens on the client: if VITE_API_URL is missing at build time, config.js falls back to http://localhost:3000 and the live site tries to call the user's own computer.
  • Vercel preview URLs: each preview deployment has a different domain, which won't match the single CLIENT_URL.
Security

CORS stops other websites from making your users' browsers call your API and read the results. It is not authentication: a script outside a browser can still call the API. That is why every quiz endpoint also requires a valid token (section 6.3).

6.3 requireAuth middleware

server/src/middlewares/requireAuth.js → requireAuth
const header = req.headers.authorization || "";
const [scheme, token] = header.split(" ");
if (scheme !== "Bearer" || !token) {
  return res.status(401).json({ error: "Not logged in" });
}
const { data, error } = await supabase.auth.getUser(token);
if (error || !data.user) {
  return res.status(401).json({ error: "Invalid or expired session" });
}
req.user = { id: data.user.id, email: data.user.email };
next();

quiz.routes.js applies it to the whole router with router.use(requireAuth), so every /api/quizzes route is protected and every controller can trust req.user.id. If Supabase itself can't be reached, the catch replies 500 "Could not verify session" instead of wrongly letting the request through.

Strings are trimmed; unknown fields dropped201, { id } of the new quiz400 { error } with the first Zod message; 401; 500 "Could not save quiz"

Also from Express itself: a body that is not valid JSON gets a 400, and a body over 100 kB (the express.json() default limit) gets a 413.

Key terms here (defined in section 3): HTTP status codes · HTTP methods (GET and POST) · REST

6.5 Socket.IO: two client sockets

The client creates two separate Socket.IO connections, each in its own module. Both use autoConnect: false, so they only connect when a page calls socket.connect() in its useEffect, and disconnect in the cleanup function when the page unmounts.

Student socketHost socket
Fileclient/src/socket/socket.jsclient/src/hostSocket.js
Used byPlayerPageHostPage
Sends a token?No (students are anonymous)Yes: auth: async (cb) => cb({ token })
Server identitysocket.data.userId = null; the player is identified by socket.idsocket.data.userId = the Supabase user ID

Why two? Students have no Supabase session, so their socket simply connects without a token and the server treats it as anonymous. The host's socket needs the token so the server can check ownership. Keeping them as two modules also means each page owns exactly one connection with its own listeners, so host and student code never interfere (for example when testing both roles in two tabs of the same browser). Because the host auth option is a function, Socket.IO calls it at every connection and reconnection, so a reconnect after an hour picks up a freshly refreshed token instead of an expired one.

client/src/hostSocket.js
const hostSocket = io(API_URL, {
  autoConnect: false,
  auth: async (cb) => {
    const { data } = await supabase.auth.getSession();
    cb({ token: data.session?.access_token ?? null });
  },
});

6.6 Handshake authentication and socket.data

Key terms here (defined in section 3): Handshake · Middleware · Singleton

socket.data is a per-connection object where the server keeps its own facts about that socket; the browser can't read or change it. io.use(fn) registers a connection middleware that runs before the connection event.

server/src/sockets/socketAuth.js → socketAuth
socket.data.userId = null;
const token = socket.handshake.auth?.token;
if (!token) return next();                 // anonymous student: allowed
const { data, error } = await supabase.auth.getUser(token);
if (!error && data.user) socket.data.userId = data.user.id;
next();                                    // never rejects the connection

Note the design: socketAuth never refuses a connection. It only labels it. Each host-only event handler then checks socket.data.userId itself. The fields stored on socket.data are:

FieldSet byMeaning
userIdsocketAuthVerified Supabase user ID, or null for students and invalid tokens
roomCodehost:create-room, host:resume, player:joinThe room this socket belongs to (cleared by host:close-room)
rolesame handlers"host" or "player"; decides what disconnect does
creatingRoomhost:create-roomTemporary flag while the quiz is loaded from the database, to block double clicks
Common mistake

The token is checked only at the handshake. If the host's access token expires an hour later, the existing socket stays authenticated until it reconnects. For a classroom quiz this is acceptable, but it is worth knowing (and saying in an interview).

6.7 Socket rooms used by QUIZZY

Socket rooms are named groups of connections on the server (remember: a "room" in this guide is QUIZZY's game object; a "socket room" is the Socket.IO group). QUIZZY uses three kinds, and choosing the right one decides who receives each message:

socket.emit(...)
Only the sender
the socket that sent the event
room:created, room:resumed, host:no-room, host:error, quiz:error, player:join:error, quiz:answer:result, quiz:answer:error
io.to(player.id)
Personal room (named by socket.id)
player A
or player B …
quiz:question, quiz:ended
io.to("483920")
Room "483920" (whole game)
host socket(s)
player A
player B
room:players, room:closed
io.to("host:483920")
Room "host:483920"
host socket(s) only
leaderboard:update
Figure 6.1: The four ways QUIZZY addresses messages, who is in each group, and which events use it.
Key idea

Four ways to send: socket.emit (only the sender), io.to(socketId) (one specific other socket, because every socket automatically joins a room named after its own ID), io.to(code) (everyone in the game) and io.to("host:" + code) (only the host's screens). The leaderboard goes to host:CODE so students never receive the whole class's scores through it, and so several host tabs all stay in sync.

Key terms here (defined in section 3): Acknowledgement · Emit · Broadcast

6.8 Every Socket.IO event

QUIZZY defines 7 events sent by clients and 13 events sent by the server, plus Socket.IO's built-in connect, connect_error and disconnect. All server handlers are inside server/src/sockets/socket.js → registerSocketHandler.

Events sent by the client

EventSent byPayloadServer handler doesSent back (and to whom)
