player:joinStudent (PlayerPage → handleJoin){ roomCode, nickname }addPlayer: room exists and is waiting; nickname is a string of 1–20 chars after trimming; same socket not already in; nickname not taken (case-insensitive). Joins the socket to room CODEplayer:join:error { message } → sender; on success room:players [players] → CODE (all students + host)
quiz:startHost (handleStartQuiz){ roomCode }startQuiz(code, socket.data.userId): room exists, requester is the host, status waiting, at least one player. Sets status playing, startedAtquiz:error → sender; on success, for each player quiz:question (question 1, no answer) → player.id; leaderboard:update → host:CODE
quiz:answerStudent (handleAnswer){ roomCode, questionIndex, optionIndex }submitAnswer(code, socket.id, …): quiz is playing; sender is a player; not finished; questionIndex equals the player's current one; option is an in-range integer. Adds 10 points if correct; advances the index; marks finished after the last onequiz:answer:error { message } → sender; or quiz:answer:result { correct, correctOption, score, nextQuestion } → sender (nextQuestion is null when finished), and leaderboard:update → host:CODE
quiz:endHost (handleEndQuiz, after a confirm dialog){ roomCode }endQuiz: requester is the host; status playing. Sets finished; computes the leaderboard; saves results with saveSessionResultsquiz:error → sender; for each player quiz:ended { rank, score, totalPlayers } → player.id; leaderboard:update (status finished) → host:CODE; if saving fails, host:error → sender

Built-in events

EventWhereWhat QUIZZY does
connectHost clientEmits host:resume. This runs on the first connection and after every automatic reconnection, which is how a host recovers after a network blip
connect_errorStudent clientOnly console.error; the student sees nothing (section 14)
disconnectServerPlayer: removePlayer; in the lobby they are removed and room:players goes to CODE; during or after the game they are marked connected: false and the leaderboard is re-sent. server/src/sockets/socket.js → emitLeaderboard (used by start, answer, end, resume, disconnect)
const emitLeaderboard = (room) => {
  io.to(`host:${room.code}`).emit("leaderboard:update", {
    status: room.status,
    totalQuestions: room.quiz.questions.length,
    players: roomService.getLeaderboard(room),
  });
};
Security

quiz:question and nextQuestion are built by question.service.js → getPublicQuestion, which copies only text and options. The correctIndex never leaves the server before the student has answered that question. Without this, any student could open the browser's developer tools, read the WebSocket messages, and see every correct answer.

Interview tip

When asked "how does the server know who to send things to?", walk through the four targets: socket.emit, io.to(socketId), io.to(code), io.to("host:"+code), and give one QUIZZY example of each. It shows you understand socket rooms rather than just "broadcasting".

7.Database

The repository contains no SQL files or migrations: the tables and the two Postgres functions were created directly in the Supabase dashboard. The tables, columns, types and foreign keys below were checked against the Supabase Table Editor. The bodies of the two Postgres functions, column defaults, indexes and RLS policy details are not visible there; those parts are marked Inferred. Exporting the schema as SQL migrations into the repository would close that gap (section 12).

7.1 Quizzes in the database, live sessions in memory

QUIZZY keeps two very different kinds of data in two different places:

Permanent dataLive game data
WhatHost accounts, quizzes, questions, final resultsRooms: code, players, scores, each player's position, status, timers
WhereSupabase PostgresThe rooms Map in server/src/services/room.service.js
LifetimeUntil deletedUntil the room is closed, or the server restarts or sleeps
SpeedA network round trip per query (tens of milliseconds)Instant (a memory lookup)
WrittenWhen a quiz is saved; once at the end of a gameOn every join, answer and disconnect

When a host creates a room, the server loads the whole quiz once from the database (quiz.service → getQuizById) and stores it inside the room object. From then on, answering a question never touches the database: submitAnswer checks the answer against room.quiz.questions in memory. When the host ends the quiz, the results are written once with session.service → saveSessionResults.

server/src/services/room.service.js → roomService (shape of a room)
const room = {
  code,          // "483920", 6 random digits, unique among live rooms
  hostId,        // Supabase user ID of the host
  quiz,          // { id, title, creatorId, questions: [{ text, options, correctIndex }] }
  players: [],   // { id: socket.id, nickname, score, currentQuestionIndex, finished, connected }
  status: "waiting",   // → "playing" → "finished"
  startedAt: null,     // set by startQuiz, saved with the results
  closeTimer: null,    // the 60-second host grace timer, if running
};
rooms.set(code, room);
Figure 7.1: Life of a room in memory. "[*]" at the end means rooms.delete(code) (closeRoom).
Real-life example

The database is the school's filing cabinet with the printed exam papers. The in-memory room is the whiteboard in the exam hall where the teacher tallies scores during the exam. At the end, the final tally is copied into the filing cabinet; then the whiteboard is wiped.

Key idea

Load once, play in memory, save once. This keeps every answer fast and keeps database traffic tiny (two queries per game), at the cost that a server restart in the middle of a game loses that game.

7.2 Tables and columns

The public schema has four tables. Every table uses a uuid primary key named id.

TableColumnTypeMeaning / used by
quizzesiduuid PKQuiz ID; checked by isValidId before any query
titletextQuiz title
created_attimestamptzCreation time; the quiz list is ordered by it (newest first). Filled by a default, since create_quiz is not given a time Inferred
creator_iduuid FKThe host who owns the quiz; a foreign key pointing to the Supabase user (auth.users.id) Inferred target. Every ownership check compares this with the token's user ID
questionsiduuid PKQuestion ID (selected, not used by the game)
quiz_iduuid FK → quizzes.idWhich quiz it belongs to; this foreign key is what lets getQuizById embed questions(...) in one query
positionintOrder inside the quiz, starting at 0
texttextThe question
optionsjsonbThe answer options as a JSON array of strings, e.g. ["wire","integer","real","time"]; arrives in JavaScript as a normal array
correct_indexintPosition of the correct option (0-based); becomes correctIndex in toQuiz
sessionsiduuid PKOne row per finished game
quiz_iduuid FK → quizzes.idWhich quiz was played (p_quiz_id)
room_codetextThe 6-digit code used (p_room_code); codes can repeat across sessions
started_attimestamptzWhen the host pressed Start (p_started_at, from room.startedAt)
ended_attimestamptzWhen results were saved. The server never sends this value, so it comes from a default or from now() inside the function Inferred
resultsiduuid PKOne row per player per game
session_iduuid FK → sessions.idWhich game the row belongs to
nicknametextPlayer nickname (players have no accounts, so there is no user ID here)
scoreint4Final score (multiples of 10)
rankint4Final rank (equal scores share a rank)
answeredintNumber of questions answered
finishedboolWhether the player reached the end before the host ended the quiz
Figure 7.2: Data model. AUTH_USERS is Supabase's built-in auth.users table (managed by Supabase Auth); the target of creator_id is inferred, all other links are foreign keys shown in the Table Editor.
Key idea

Two pairs of tables, the same shape twice: a parent with one row per thing (quizzes, sessions) and a child with many rows pointing back to it (questions, results). Each pair is written in one go by one Postgres function, so a parent never exists without its children.

Common mistake

Mixing up naming styles. The database uses snake_case (correct_index, creator_id) while JavaScript uses camelCase (correctIndex, creatorId). quiz.service → toQuiz converts on the way out, but on the way in create_quiz receives the JavaScript objects as JSON, so inside the function the key is correctIndex, not correct_index. Getting this wrong silently stores NULL or fails the insert.

Key terms here (defined in section 3): Primary key · Foreign key · One-to-many relationship · JOIN · UUID

7.3 Queries: which server function runs what

Server functionQuery (supabase-js)Called from
quiz.service → listQuizzes(creatorId)from("quizzes").select("id, title, created_at, questions(count)").eq("creator_id", creatorId).order("created_at", { ascending: false }). questions(count) counts each quiz's questions in the same queryGET /api/quizzes
quiz.service → getQuizById(id)from("quizzes").select("id, title, creator_id, questions(id, position, text, options, correct_index)").eq("id", id).order("position", { referencedTable: "questions" }).maybeSingle(). One query returns the quiz with its questions in orderGET /api/quizzes/:id; socket host:create-room
quiz.service → createQuiz(...)rpc("create_quiz", { p_creator_id, p_title, p_questions })POST /api/quizzes
session.service → saveSessionResults(...)rpc("save_session_results", { p_quiz_id, p_room_code, p_started_at, p_results })socket quiz:end
requireAuth, socketAuthauth.getUser(token) (Supabase Auth, not a table query)every REST request; every socket connection with a token

toQuiz in quiz.service.js converts database names (snake_case like creator_id) into JavaScript names (camelCase like creatorId), so the rest of the server never sees database column names.

Security

supabase-js sends every value as a parameter, never by pasting text into SQL, so a quiz titled '); DROP TABLE quizzes; -- is stored as a harmless string. This prevents SQL injection.

7.4 Postgres functions and transactions

Key terms here (defined in section 3): Transaction · ACID · Database function (RPC)

Why QUIZZY uses functions here: saving a quiz writes one row into quizzes and N rows into questions. With two separate insert calls from Node, a failure in between (bad data in question 7, network drop) would leave a quiz with no questions. supabase-js cannot run a multi-statement transaction from the client, so the inserts are moved into a Postgres function. The same reasoning applies to save_session_results (one game row plus one row per player). It is also one network round trip instead of several.

create_quiz

Called with p_creator_id (from the verified token, never from the request body), p_title and p_questions: the Zod-cleaned array [{ text, options, correctIndex }] sent as JSON. It returns the new quiz's ID, which the controller sends back as 201 { id }. The real function body isn't visible in the Table Editor; a body matching the real tables (0-based position, jsonb options) would look like this Illustrative:

create function create_quiz(p_creator_id uuid, p_title text, p_questions jsonb)
returns uuid language plpgsql as $$
declare new_id uuid;
begin
  insert into quizzes (creator_id, title) values (p_creator_id, p_title)
  returning id into new_id;

  insert into questions (quiz_id, position, text, options, correct_index)
  select new_id,
         q.ord - 1,                           -- position starts at 0
         q.item->>'text',
         q.item->'options',                   -- jsonb array, stored as is
         (q.item->>'correctIndex')::int     -- camelCase key, as sent by Node
  from jsonb_array_elements(p_questions) with ordinality as q(item, ord);

  return new_id;
end $$;

save_session_results

Called once from the quiz:end handler with p_quiz_id, p_room_code, p_started_at (ISO timestamp from room.startedAt) and p_results, an array of { nickname, score, rank, answered, finished }. Note what session.service.js deliberately leaves out: the socket IDs and the connected flag, which mean nothing after the game. It inserts one row into sessions and one row per player into results, all in one transaction. A matching body would look like this Illustrative:

create function save_session_results(p_quiz_id uuid, p_room_code text,
                                     p_started_at timestamptz, p_results jsonb)
returns uuid language plpgsql as $$
declare new_session uuid;
begin
  insert into sessions (quiz_id, room_code, started_at, ended_at)
  values (p_quiz_id, p_room_code, p_started_at, now())
  returning id into new_session;

  insert into results (session_id, nickname, score, rank, answered, finished)
  select new_session, r->>'nickname', (r->>'score')::int, (r->>'rank')::int,
         (r->>'answered')::int, (r->>'finished')::boolean
  from jsonb_array_elements(p_results) as r;

  return new_session;
end $$;

If the call fails, the game still ends normally for students and the host gets host:error "The quiz ended, but the results could not be saved". Because it is one transaction, a failure never leaves a sessions row without its results.

7.5 Secret key vs publishable key

Publishable keySecret key
VariableVITE_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY (Vercel / client/.env)SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY (Render / server/.env)
Used inclient/src/supabase/supabaseClient.jsserver/src/db/supaBase.js
Is it secret?No. It is bundled into the JavaScript every visitor downloadsYes. Never sent to a browser, never committed
PowerActs as an anonymous or logged-in user; table access is limited by Row Level SecurityFull access; bypasses Row Level Security
QUIZZY uses it forSign up, log in, sessions, sign outVerifying tokens and every table read/write

(Older Supabase projects call these the anon key and the service_role key.) The server client is created with persistSession: false, autoRefreshToken: false and detectSessionInUrl: false because a server has no browser storage, URL or logged-in user of its own.

Common mistake

Putting the secret key in a VITE_ variable "to make it work". Anything named VITE_* is published inside the client bundle, so anyone could read it and get full control of the database. Another easy slip: naming the variable differently on Render than in code (SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY vs SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY). supaBase.js throws "Missing SUPABASE_URL or SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY" at startup, which is good: it fails loudly instead of half-working.

7.6 Row Level Security (RLS)

Key terms here (defined in section 3): Row Level Security (RLS) · Secret key vs publishable key · Defense in depth

What the code tells us: the browser never queries tables (it only uses supabase.auth), and the server uses the secret key, which bypasses RLS anyway. So the safest correct configuration is RLS enabled with no policies on every table: the server keeps working, and the publishable key opens nothing.

The Table Editor shows an "Add RLS policy" button on all four tables, which is the prompt Supabase shows for tables that have RLS switched on but no policies yet, rather than an "RLS disabled" warning. That suggests QUIZZY already uses exactly this configuration Likely; confirm it under Authentication → Policies, where each table should show RLS as enabled with no policies.

Security

Because the publishable key is public, if RLS were disabled on questions, anyone could call Supabase's REST API directly with that key and download every quiz, including the correct answers, completely bypassing QUIZZY's server and its answer hiding. Check this in the Supabase dashboard (Table Editor shows "RLS disabled" warnings).

7.7 Indexes

Key terms here (defined in section 3): Index (database)

Which indexes exist beyond the automatic primary-key ones is not visible in the Table Editor Unknown. The queries above would benefit from quizzes(creator_id, created_at desc) (the quiz list) and questions(quiz_id, position) (loading a quiz in order), and results(session_id) for a future "past sessions" page. At classroom scale (a few hundred rows) the difference is invisible, but naming them is a good interview answer.

Interview tip

"Why a Postgres function?" is a favourite question. Answer: "Saving a quiz writes to two tables, quizzes and questions. I needed it to be atomic, and supabase-js can't open a transaction from Node, so I moved the inserts into a Postgres function and call it with RPC. One call, one transaction, all-or-nothing." Then mention that the creator ID comes from the verified token, never from the request body.

8.Authentication and authorization

Key terms here (defined in section 3): Authentication · Authorization · Session · Access token · Refresh token · JWT (JSON Web Token)

8.1 Sign-up and login in the browser

LoginPage has one form with two modes (mode = "signin" or "signup"). On submit, LoginPage → handleSubmit calls Supabase Auth directly from the browser; the QUIZZY server is not involved:

client/src/pages/LoginPage.jsx → handleSubmit
const { data, error } = isSignup
  ? await supabase.auth.signUp({ email, password })
  : await supabase.auth.signInWithPassword({ email, password });
if (error) { setError(error.message); return; }
navigate(redirectTo, { replace: true });   // redirectTo = location.state?.from ?? "/host"

Supabase stores the password (hashed) and returns a session. supabase-js saves the session in the browser's localStorage and refreshes the access token automatically before it expires. The form also enforces minLength={6} on the password, matching Supabase's default minimum.

Email confirmation is a Supabase project setting, not visible in the code:

  • If it is off: signUp returns a session immediately; the host lands on /host, logged in.
  • If it is on: signUp succeeds but returns no session until the email link is clicked. handleSubmit still navigates to /host, RequireAuth finds no user and sends the host back to /login with no explanation (listed in section 14).

8.2 AuthContext and RequireAuth

Key terms here (defined in section 3): Context (React) · Custom hook

  • AuthContext.jsx → AuthProvider: on mount, reads the saved session with getSession() (then sets loading = false), and subscribes to onAuthStateChange so login, logout and token refreshes update React state everywhere. It exposes { session, user, loading, signOut }.
  • RequireAuth.jsx: while loading, shows a spinner (so a logged-in host isn't wrongly bounced to login during the first instant); if there is no user, returns <Navigate to="/login" replace state={{ from: location.pathname }} />; otherwise renders the page. from lets the login page send the host back where they were going.
  • QuizListPage shows user.email and calls signOut, which clears the session; onAuthStateChange fires, user becomes null, and RequireAuth redirects to login.

8.3 Sessions and JWTs end to end

Figure 8.1: One token, two transports. The server never sees the password.

8.4 How hosts are identified

A host is always identified by the Supabase user ID taken from a verified token, never by anything the client claims:

  • Creating a quiz: quiz.controller → createQuiz calls quizService.createQuiz({ creatorId: req.user.id, ...result.data }). A malicious body containing creatorId is harmless only because Zod's quizSchema drops unknown fields: note that the spread comes after creatorId, so if the schema ever allowed extra keys, a body value would override the real ID. Putting creatorId last would make this safe by construction (section 14).
  • Creating a room: roomService(userId, quiz) stores hostId = socket.data.userId.
  • Host-only events compare room.hostId with socket.data.userId.
  • Finding your room again: findRoomByHost(userId) loops over all rooms. This is what makes refresh-and-resume work: a new socket, with a new socket.id, but the same user ID.

Students, by contrast, are identified only by socket.id: a random ID that exists for one connection. That is enough for an anonymous classroom game, but it means a student who loses their connection becomes a new, unknown socket (section 12).

8.5 Every authorization rule

ActionWho may do itEnforced inIf not allowed
Any /api/quizzes requestLogged-in usersrequireAuth via router.use401
List quizzesOwner sees only their ownlistQuizzes: .eq("creator_id", req.user.id)(simply not listed)
Read one quiz (with answers)Owner onlygetQuiz: quiz.creatorId !== req.user.id404 "Quiz not found"
Save a quizAny logged-in user, as themselvescreateQuiz: creatorId: req.user.id-
Generate with AIAny logged-in user; max 10 / hour (intended)requireAuth; aiRateLimit (not reached, section 14)401 / 429
Create a roomLogged-in owner of the quiz; one room per host at a time; quiz must have questionssocket.js host:create-roomhost:error "Quiz not found" / "You already have a running room" / …
Resume a roomIts host (by user ID)host:resume → findRoomByHost(userId)host:no-room
Start / end the quizThe room's hostroom.service → startQuiz, endQuiz: room.hostId !== requesterIdquiz:error "Only the host can …"
Close the roomThe room's hosthost:close-room: role === "host" and room.hostId === userIdIgnored (just acknowledged)
Join a roomAnyone with the code, while the room is waiting, with a free 1–20 character nicknameroom.service → addPlayerplayer:join:error
AnswerSockets that joined as players, for their current question only, while playingroom.service → submitAnswerquiz:answer:error

8.6 Why "not yours" returns 404, not 403

When host A asks for host B's quiz, getQuiz answers 404 Not Found, exactly the same as for a quiz that doesn't exist; the socket handler likewise says "Quiz not found". A 403 Forbidden would confirm "this quiz exists, you just can't see it", which leaks information and lets an attacker probe which IDs are real (enumeration). Returning 404 for both cases reveals nothing. GitHub does the same for private repositories.

Security

Without the ownership check, any logged-in host who obtained another quiz's ID could load it with all the correct answers, or open a room with someone else's quiz. Quiz IDs are random UUIDs and hard to guess, but security should not depend on secrecy of IDs; the ownership check makes guessing pointless.

Interview tip

Separate the layers clearly: "Supabase handles authentication and issues JWTs. My server verifies each token with getUser, then does authorization itself: ownership of quizzes via creator_id, and ownership of rooms via hostId. The React RequireAuth is only for user experience."

9.End-to-end flows

This section follows real actions through the whole system. Each flow has a sequence diagram (time runs downward; arrows are messages) and numbered steps naming the exact file and function. Dashed arrows are replies.

Key terms here (defined in section 3): Sequence diagram

9.1 Host signs up and logs in

Figure 9.1: Sign up / log in, then the first authenticated request.
  1. The teacher opens /host (or clicks "Go to your dashboard" on HomePage). App.jsx wraps that route in RequireAuth.
  2. auth/RequireAuth.jsx reads useAuth(). While AuthProvider is still loading the saved session it shows a spinner; with no user it redirects to /login, remembering from: "/host".
  3. pages/LoginPage.jsx → handleSubmit calls supabase.auth.signUp (sign-up mode) or signInWithPassword (log-in mode). Errors such as "Invalid login credentials" are shown with ErrorMessage.
  4. On success, supabase-js stores the session; AuthContext.jsx's onAuthStateChange listener sets the new session, and handleSubmit navigates to from.
  5. QuizListPage's useEffect → loadQuizzes calls apiFetch("/api/quizzes"); the server runs requireAuth, then quiz.controller → listQuizzes → quiz.service → listQuizzes(req.user.id).

9.2 Host creates a quiz manually

  1. QuizListPage → "Create a new quiz" links to /host/new (CreateQuizPage).
  2. The page starts with one empty question from emptyQuestion(): a random id (crypto.randomUUID(), used only as a React key), empty text, four empty options and correctIndex: 0.
  3. Typing calls updateQuestion / updateOption, which copy the array and change one field (immutable updates, so React notices the change). The radio button sets correctIndex. addQuestion / removeQuestion add or filter by id.
  4. Save submits the form: handleSubmit sends POST /api/quizzes with { title, questions }. The temporary id fields are included, but Zod strips them on the server.
  5. Server: requireAuth → quiz.controller → createQuiz → quizSchema.safeParse(req.body). If invalid, the first problem is returned as 400 { error } (e.g. "Options cannot be empty") and shown in the sticky Save bar.
  6. If valid, quiz.service → createQuiz calls the create_quiz Postgres function: one transaction inserts the quiz and all its questions. The controller replies 201 { id }.
  7. The client navigates back to /host, which reloads the list.

9.3 Host creates a quiz with AI (generate → review → save)

Figure 9.3: AI generation never saves anything by itself; the host always reviews and then saves.
  1. CreateQuizPage → handleGenerate: if any question already has text, it asks window.confirm("Replace your current questions with AI-generated ones?"). It then sets generating (spinner, "This can take a few seconds.") and sends topic, difficulty and count: Number(aiCount).
  2. Server: requireAuth, then quiz.controller → generateQuiz validates with ai.schema → generateRequestSchema (topic 3–100 chars, difficulty in the allowlist, count 1–15).
  3. ai.service → generateQuestions builds the prompt with buildPrompt: exactly 4 options, one correct, vary the correct position, plausible distractors, no "all of the above", length limits.
  4. It calls ai.models.generateContent with responseMimeType: "application/json" and responseJsonSchema (an object with a questions array of { text, options, correctIndex }), wrapped in callWithRetry: on HTTP 429, 500 or 503 from Gemini it waits 1 s, then 2 s (exponential backoff), up to 2 retries.
  5. The response text is parsed with JSON.parse and checked with generatedSchema (which reuses questionSchema). If it fails, a second full attempt is made. After 2 failed attempts it throws "AI returned invalid questions", and the controller replies 502.
  6. On success the questions are cut to the requested count (.slice(0, input.count)) and returned. Nothing is saved yet.
  7. The page replaces its questions (giving each a new React key) and, if the title is empty, uses the topic as the title. The calm note "AI can make mistakes. Review each question…" stays visible.
  8. The host edits anything wrong and clicks Save: from here it is exactly flow 9.2, steps 4–7. Human and AI questions pass the same questionSchema.
Key idea

The AI's output is treated as untrusted input: structured output narrows its format, Zod verifies it, invalid output triggers a retry, and a human reviews it before it is ever saved.

9.4 Host creates a room; student joins

Figure 9.4: Creating a room and joining it.
  1. Host clicks Host on a quiz card → /host/:quizId. HostPage's useEffect registers listeners and calls socket.connect() on hostSocket; the auth callback attaches the current token.
  2. Server: socketAuth verifies the token and sets socket.data.userId. On the client, the connect event triggers handleConnect → host:resume. No room exists, so the server answers host:no-room and the page shows Create room.
  3. handleCreateRoom emits host:create-room { quizId }. The handler in socket.js checks login, "already has a room" (on this socket, via the creatingRoom flag, and across all rooms with findRoomByHost), and the UUID format.
  4. It loads the quiz with quiz.service → getQuizById. After the await it re-checks: is the socket still connected? Does this user own the quiz? Does it have questions? Did another tab create a room meanwhile?
  5. room.service → roomService creates the room with a random unused 6-digit code (generateRoomCode loops until the code is free). The socket joins rooms CODE and host:CODE; socket.data.role = "host".
  6. room:created → handleRoomCreated stores the code and title. The lobby shows joinLink = window.location.origin + "/join/" + code, the giant code and <QRCodeSVG value={joinLink} />.
  7. Student, via QR: the phone camera opens https://<site>/join/483920. Vercel's rewrite serves index.html; React Router renders PlayerPage with code from useParams(). Via the home page: HomePage accepts digits only (replace(/\D/g, "")), enables Join at exactly 6 digits, and handleJoin navigates to /join/:code.
  8. PlayerPage connects the anonymous student socket. The student types a nickname; handleJoin trims it, refuses an empty one locally, and emits player:join { roomCode: code, nickname }.
  9. room.service → addPlayer validates (room exists and is waiting, nickname 1–20 chars and not taken case-insensitively, socket not already in) and pushes { id: socket.id, nickname, score: 0, currentQuestionIndex: 0, finished: false, connected: true }. Errors go back as player:join:error (e.g. "That nickname is already taken").
  10. On success the socket joins room CODE and the server sends room:players to the whole room. The student's handlePlayers sets joined = true (that is how the student knows the join worked) and shows the lobby; the host's lobby gets a new pill.

9.5 Quiz starts; students answer; live leaderboard

Figure 9.5: The answer loop. Each student runs this loop at their own speed.
  1. The Start button is disabled until players.length > 0. handleStartQuiz emits quiz:start { roomCode }.
  2. room.service → startQuiz checks the requester is the host (room.hostId === socket.data.userId), the room is waiting, and there is at least one player; then sets status = "playing" and startedAt = Date.now(). Joining is now closed (addPlayer rejects with "This quiz has already started").
  3. For each player, the server emits quiz:question to that player's personal room (io.to(player.id)) with question.service → getPublicQuestion: { index, total, question: { text, options } }, without the answer. emitLeaderboard sends the first board to host:CODE, and the host screen switches to the leaderboard.
  4. Student taps a tile: PlayerPage → handleAnswer ignores the tap if already submitting or showing a result; otherwise it marks the tile, sets submitting, and emits quiz:answer { roomCode, questionIndex: currentQuestion.index, optionIndex }.
  5. room.service → submitAnswer validates: room exists and is playing; the sender is a player; not finished; questionIndex === player.currentQuestionIndex (blocks double answers and skipping ahead); optionIndex is an integer within the options. Then it scores (POINTS_PER_CORRECT = 10), increments currentQuestionIndex, and sets finished after the last question.
  6. The sender gets quiz:answer:result: correct, correctOption (now safe to reveal), the new score, and nextQuestion (the public version of the next question, or null). QuestionView shows the green ring and checkmark on the correct option and a red ring and cross on a wrong pick.
  7. The host gets a new leaderboard:update. room.service → getLeaderboard sorts by score (ties by nickname) and gives equal scores the same rank (findIndex of the first player with that score, plus one); answered is the player's currentQuestionIndex. Leaderboard.jsx's motion.li layout slides rows to their new places.
  8. The student clicks Next question: handleNext simply displays result.nextQuestion; there is no extra round trip because the server already advanced the player. When nextQuestion is null, the button says "See my score" and leads to the "You finished!" screen.
Security

The score is computed only on the server. The client sends which option was chosen, never "I was correct" or "my score is 100". Without this, a student could edit the JavaScript in their browser and send themselves any score.

9.6 Host ends the quiz; final ranks; results saved

Figure 9.6: Ending a quiz and saving the results.
  1. "End quiz" is only shown while leaderboard.status === "playing". handleEndQuiz asks for confirmation, then emits quiz:end { roomCode }.
  2. room.service → endQuiz checks host and playing status and sets finished. Students who had not finished simply stop where they are.
  3. The final leaderboard is computed once. Each player gets their own quiz:ended { rank, score, totalPlayers }; PlayerPage → handleQuizEnded shows the big rank, with a medal for ranks 1–3.
  4. The host gets leaderboard:update with status: "finished": Leaderboard.jsx shows "Final results", a podium for the top 3, then the rest.
  5. session.service → saveSessionResults calls the save_session_results Postgres function. On failure, the error is logged and the host is told via host:error; the game result on screen is unaffected.
  6. "Back to my quizzes" → handleCloseRoom → socket.timeout(3000).emit("host:close-room", ack). The server deletes the room (no room:closed, because students already have their final screen) and calls the ack; the client navigates to /host (also after 3 s if the server never answers).

9.7 Host refresh, student disconnect, closing the room

Figure 9.7: The 60-second grace period (HOST_GRACE_MS = 60 * 1000).

Host refreshes mid-quiz

  1. The old page unmounts or the network drops; the server's disconnect handler sees socket.data.role === "host".
  2. It counts how many sockets are still in host:CODE (io.sockets.adapter.rooms.get(...)?.size). If another host tab is open, nothing happens. Otherwise it starts a 60-second timer stored in room.closeTimer. The game keeps running: students can keep answering.
  3. The reloaded HostPage connects a new socket (same user, fresh token). On connect it emits host:resume; the server finds the room with findRoomByHost(userId), cancels the timer, re-joins both socket rooms, and sends room:resumed plus, if the game has started, the current leaderboard:update. The screen returns to exactly where it was.
  4. If the host never returns, the timer callback first checks the room is still the same object (getRoom(room.code) !== room guards against a deleted or replaced room), sends room:closed to all students (unless the quiz is already finished), and deletes the room.

A student disconnects

  1. disconnect with role "player" calls room.service → removePlayer(code, socket.id).
  2. In the lobby (waiting), the player is removed from the list and room:players is re-sent, so their pill disappears and their nickname is free again.
  3. During or after the game, the player is kept (their score still counts) but marked connected: false; the host's board fades the row and shows "(disconnected)". On the client, Leaderboard.jsx's allFinished check ("Everyone has finished!") counts disconnected players as done.
  4. There is no way back in: a reconnecting phone has a new socket.id, and addPlayer rejects joins once the quiz has started (section 12).

Host closes the room

  1. From the lobby ("Close room", after a confirm) or the final results ("Back to my quizzes"), handleCloseRoom emits host:close-room with an acknowledgement and a 3-second timeout.
  2. The server verifies role === "host" and room.hostId === userId, cancels any timer, sends room:closed if the quiz isn't finished (students see the calm "Session ended" screen), deletes the room, leaves both socket rooms and clears socket.data.
  3. The ack fires and the host goes back to /host. Now findRoomByHost finds nothing, so the host can create a new room.
Real-life example

The grace period is like a teacher stepping out of the exam hall: the exam keeps going, and if they come back within a minute nothing changes. If they don't come back, the invigilator sends everyone home.

Interview tip

"How do you handle a host refreshing the page?" is a great question to be asked, because QUIZZY has a real answer: identity by user ID instead of socket ID, host:resume on every connect, and a 60-second grace timer with a stale-room guard. Mention the trade-off: students don't have this yet, because they have no stable identity.

10.Deployment

In production the client and server are deployed separately, both automatically from the same GitHub repository. Dashboard settings are not stored in the repository, so the values below marked Assumed describe the standard setup for this project layout. Check them against your Vercel and Render dashboards.

This one rule makes the SPA work on Vercel: any path that is not a real file (/host, /join/483920) is answered with index.html, and React Router then picks the page. Real files such as /assets/index-abc123.js are still served normally.

10.3 Every environment variable

NameSet inRead byPurpose / notes

Both .env files are listed in .gitignore (root and client/.gitignore), and the Git history confirms no .env file has ever been committed.

Common mistake
  • Wrong variable names. The client only sees variables that start with VITE_; naming it API_URL on Vercel gives undefined and the localhost fallback. On the server, a typo such as GEMINI_KEY stops the server at startup with "Missing GEMINI_API_KEY or GEMINI_MODEL in .env". The message mentions .env even on Render, where the fix is in the dashboard.
  • Localhost values in production. Copying VITE_API_URL=http://localhost:3000 into Vercel means the live site calls the visitor's own laptop.
  • ?? versus ||. config.js uses ??, which only replaces null/undefined. If the variable exists but is an empty string, API_URL becomes "" and requests go to the Vercel site itself.
  • Forgetting to redeploy the client after changing a VITE_ variable (see Vite in section 3.10).

10.4 Why the server can't run on Vercel

Key terms here (defined in section 3): Serverless function · Long-running process

QUIZZY's server breaks all three serverless assumptions:

  1. Long-lived connections. A Socket.IO connection stays open for the whole game (minutes). Serverless functions end shortly after responding and cannot host a WebSocket server.
  2. State in memory. The rooms Map must survive between events. In serverless, the next event could reach a different, fresh copy with an empty Map.
  3. Timers. The 60-second host grace timer (setTimeout) needs a process that is still running a minute later.

Render runs node server.js as one continuously running process, which is exactly what this design needs.

10.5 Continuous deployment from GitHub

Key terms here (defined in section 3): Continuous deployment · Production vs preview · Deployment

Both platforms are connected to the GitHub repository. A push to main makes Vercel rebuild client/ and Render rebuild and restart server/. Two consequences:

  • A server deploy restarts the process, which deletes every live room. Avoid pushing during a class.
  • Commits like deployement chnages and chore: trigger Vercel deploy in the history show the usual early-deployment loop: fix a setting, push, check.

10.6 HTTPS and wss://

Vercel and Render both provide HTTPS certificates. Render's proxy handles the encryption (TLS) and forwards plain HTTP to the Node process on PORT, so the code never touches certificates. When VITE_API_URL starts with https://, socket.io-client automatically uses wss:// for the WebSocket upgrade.

Common mistake

Using http:// for VITE_API_URL in production. A page loaded over HTTPS may not open http:// or ws:// connections (mixed content), so the browser silently blocks every API call and socket.

10.7 Free-tier sleep behaviour

Render's free web services spin down after about 15 minutes without incoming traffic. The next request wakes the service, which can take up to around a minute (a cold start). Because rooms live in memory, a spin-down or restart also deletes every room.

  • What users see: the host's quiz list spinner hangs for a while; a host socket may take a long time to connect ("Checking for a running session...").
  • Workaround: open the host dashboard a few minutes before class; the GET /api/quizzes call wakes the server. The health route GET / can be used to wake it too.
  • Supabase's free plan can also pause projects after a long period of inactivity, and Gemini's free tier has request quotas, which is one reason callWithRetry retries on HTTP 429.
Interview tip

Mention the cold start yourself, before you are asked: "The free tier sleeps; in production I'd use a paid always-on instance, because a sleep or redeploy also wipes the in-memory rooms." It shows you understand the link between hosting and your state design.

11.Security measures

Each protection below names where it lives, what attack it prevents, and what would happen without it.

ProtectionWherePreventsWithout it
Answer hidingquestion.service → getPublicQuestionReading correct answers from WebSocket trafficAny student could open DevTools and see every correctIndex
Server-side scoringroom.service → submitAnswerClients claiming pointsA modified client could send "score: 1000"
Question-order check (questionIndex === currentQuestionIndex)submitAnswerAnswering the same question twice, replaying messages, skipping aheadResend the correct answer 50 times for 500 points
Option bounds checksubmitAnswer (Number.isInteger, range)Malformed indexes ("2", -1, 99)Wrong-type comparisons; nonsense data in results
Join rules: only while waiting; nickname 1–20 chars, must be a string, unique (case-insensitive)room.service → addPlayerLate joiners, impersonation ("Ana" vs "ana"), huge or non-string nicknamesTwo "Ana"s on the board; a 10,000-character name breaking the projector layout
Escaped outputReact (no dangerouslySetInnerHTML anywhere)XSS: a nickname like <img src=x onerror=…>Script running on the host's (logged-in) machine via the projector page
Input validation (Zod)quiz.schema.js, ai.schema.jsMalformed, oversized or inconsistent quizzes and requestsA quiz with correctIndex: 7 of 4 options would break the game later
Field allowlistsz.object strips unknown keys; explicit select(...) columns; toQuiz; getLeaderboard; saveSessionResults mappingMass assignment (extra fields like creatorId) and leaking internal fieldsClients could set fields they shouldn't; socket IDs saved to the DB
ID validationquiz.service → isValidIdMalformed IDs reaching the databaseDatabase errors turned into 500s; noisy probing
AuthenticationrequireAuth (REST), socketAuth + per-event checks (sockets)Anonymous use of host featuresAnyone could list, create, or host quizzes
Ownership checks + 404getQuiz, host:create-room, startQuiz, endQuiz, host:close-roomUsing or controlling other hosts' quizzes and rooms; ID enumerationA student who learns the code could start or end the game
Identity from the tokencreateQuiz (creatorId: req.user.id), roomService(userId, …)Creating quizzes as someone elseSpoofed ownership
Race-condition guardshost:create-room: creatingRoom flag, re-check after await, socket.connectedDouble rooms from double clicks or two tabsTwo rooms for one host; orphan rooms
AI input limitsgenerateRequestSchema (topic ≤ 100 chars, difficulty enum, count ≤ 15)Cost abuse and very long promptsAsking for 10,000 questions per call
AI output validationai.service: JSON schema + generatedSchema + retry + human reviewMalformed or nonsensical AI output reaching the databaseQuestions with no correct answer saved and played
Socket payload validation (missing)Should be in every socket.on handlerMalformed messages from any clientThis is the current state: one payload-less quiz:start crashes the server (section 14, issue 1)
Rate limiting (10/hour/user)aiRateLimit.jsDraining the Gemini quota / billThis is the current state: the limiter is never reached (section 14)
CORS allowlistapp.js, server.js (CLIENT_URL)Other websites using visitors' browsers to call the APIAny site could script requests from a logged-in host's browser
Secret key on the server only; .env git-ignoreddb/supaBase.js, .gitignoreFull database takeoverAnyone reading the bundle or repo controls the database
Parameterized queriessupabase-js / RPCSQL injectionCrafted titles could run SQL
Generic error messagesAll catch blocks reply with fixed text; details only in console.errorLeaking stack traces, table names, keysAttackers learn the internals from error responses
HTTPS / WSSVercel, RenderEavesdropping on tokens and answersTokens readable on school Wi-Fi
Body size limitexpress.json() default 100 kB, plus Zod's array limitsMemory exhaustion with giant bodiesOne request could slow the server for everyone
