Security

The guiding rule is never trust the client. Everything the browser sends (nicknames, answers, quiz data, room codes) is checked on the server, and everything the server sends is the minimum the browser needs. The AI is treated the same way: its output is untrusted input.

Common mistake

Thinking the front-end checks are security. The Start button being disabled with 0 players, RequireAuth, and the 6-digit check on HomePage are all convenience; anyone can bypass them. Each one has a matching server check (startQuiz, requireAuth, addPlayer).

Interview tip

Pick three and explain them deeply: answer hiding (what's in the payload and why), server-side scoring with the question-index check (replay attacks), and the 404-instead-of-403 ownership check. Then volunteer one weakness (the rate limiter bug) and how you would fix it. Honesty about a flaw scores better than claiming perfection.

12.Known limitations and future improvements

LimitationWhy it existsImprovement
Single server instanceRooms live in one process's memory; socket rooms exist only in that processMove room state to Redis and use the Socket.IO Redis adapter so several instances share rooms and broadcasts
Rooms lost on restart, deploy or sleepIn-memory design (decision 2 in DECISIONS.md)Persist room snapshots (Redis or Postgres); paid always-on instance; deploy outside class times
Students can't reconnectPlayers are identified by socket.id; joins are closed once playingGive each player a random playerId stored in sessionStorage, send it on join, and add a player:rejoin event that re-attaches the new socket
No feedback when the server is unreachableconnect_error only logs; the host spinner never endsShow a "Can't reach the server, retrying…" message; a timeout on the "Checking" screen
Simple scoringFixed 10 points per correct answer, no time elementSpeed bonus, streaks, per-question time limits (server-timed)
No editing or deleting quizzesOnly list, create and (unused) get endpoints existPUT/DELETE /api/quizzes/:id with the same ownership check; an edit page using GET /:id
Saved results are never shownsave_session_results fills sessions and results, but no endpoint or page reads themA "Past sessions" page with per-question statistics for teachers
One room per hostfindRoomByHost returns one room; resume ignores which quiz you openedKey rooms by host + quiz, or show "You have a running room for X: resume or close?"
Rate limiter in memory (and currently bypassed)A Map in one process; duplicate routeFix the route; move counts to Redis or a database table so limits survive restarts and multiple instances
Token checked only at socket handshakesocketAuth runs once per connectionRe-verify on sensitive events or disconnect sockets when the token expires
A network call per authenticated requestauth.getUser(token) asks Supabase every timeVerify the JWT locally with the project's signing keys (JWKS) and cache results
Errors shown with alert() on the host pageQuick implementationInline error banners, like the student side
No automated tests or CI"test": "echo \"Error: no test specified\""Unit tests for room.service (pure functions, easy to test), Socket.IO integration tests, GitHub Actions running lint and tests before deploy
Database schema not in the repoCreated in the Supabase dashboardSupabase CLI migrations committed to Git, so the database can be recreated and reviewed
Fixed four options in the editoremptyQuestion() always creates 4; the server allows 2–6Add/remove option buttons; the student grid already handles any count
Key idea

Almost every limitation traces back to one deliberate trade-off: in-memory, single-process game state. It made the first version simple and fast; the "next step" for most improvements is a shared store such as Redis.

Interview tip

When asked "how would you scale this to 10,000 concurrent games?", answer in steps: (1) move room state to Redis, (2) add the Socket.IO Redis adapter, (3) run several Render instances behind a load balancer with sticky sessions, (4) give players stable IDs so reconnects can land on any instance.

13.Interview questions with answers

58 questions in four groups. The answers are written the way you would say them about your project: specific, with the reason and the trade-off. Don't memorize them word for word; make sure you can explain each idea and point to the file.

Interview tip

A strong answer has three parts: what you did (with a concrete name from the code), why (the problem it solves), and the trade-off (what it costs or what you'd do at larger scale).

13.1 Basic

Q1.What is QUIZZY, in two sentences?

A student-paced live quiz app: teachers create multiple-choice quizzes, by hand or with Gemini, open a room with a 6-digit code and QR code, and students join from their phones and answer at their own speed. The teacher sees a live leaderboard with scores and progress, and the final results are saved to Postgres.

Q2.What is the tech stack and where does each part run?

React 19 with Vite, React Router and Tailwind v4 on the client, deployed as static files on Vercel. Node.js with Express 5 and Socket.IO on the server, running as one long-lived process on Render. Supabase provides Postgres and authentication, and Gemini generates questions. The browser only talks to Supabase for login; all data goes through my server.

Q3.Why do you use both REST and WebSockets?

REST is for actions the user starts and that have one answer: list quizzes, save a quiz, generate with AI (/api/quizzes). The live game needs the server to push updates the moment someone else acts, like a student joining or answering, so it uses a persistent Socket.IO connection. Using REST for the game would mean polling, which adds delay and wasted requests.

Q4.Why Socket.IO rather than plain WebSockets?

Socket.IO gives me named events (quiz:answer), rooms for broadcasting (io.to(code)), automatic reconnection (which my host resume relies on), acknowledgements (used by host:close-room), a handshake auth payload for the token, and a fallback to HTTP long-polling. With raw WebSockets I'd have to build all of that myself.

Q5.How does a student join a game?

They scan the QR code, which is just the URL /join/<code>, or type the code on the home page. PlayerPage connects an anonymous socket and emits player:join with the code and nickname. room.service → addPlayer checks the room exists and is still waiting, and that the nickname is 1–20 characters and not taken; then the server broadcasts room:players to the room, and receiving that list is how the student's page knows it has joined.

Q6.How are room codes generated? What about collisions?

generateRoomCode picks a random number from 100000 to 999999 and loops until it finds one that isn't already a key in the rooms Map, so live codes never collide. Six digits are easy to read on a projector and type on a phone. They are not secret (anyone in the class sees them), which is fine because joining only gives you a player seat; host actions need the host's token.

Q7.What does the useEffect in PlayerPage do, and why is there a cleanup function?

It registers all socket listeners (room:players, quiz:question, …) and calls socket.connect() once when the page mounts. The cleanup removes every listener with socket.off and disconnects. Without the cleanup, navigating away and back would add duplicate listeners, so each event would be handled twice, and the socket would stay connected as a ghost player.

Q8.Which environment variables does the app need?

On Vercel: VITE_API_URL, VITE_SUPABASE_URL, VITE_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY. They need the VITE_ prefix to reach browser code and are baked in at build time. On Render: CLIENT_URL for CORS, SUPABASE_URL, SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY, GEMINI_MODEL; PORT is set by Render. The server throws at startup if a required one is missing, so misconfiguration fails loudly.

Q9.What is CORS and why does QUIZZY need it?

Browsers block a page from reading responses from a different origin unless that server allows it. My page is on Vercel and my API on Render, which are different origins, so the server sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin for exactly CLIENT_URL, in Express (app.js) and in the Socket.IO server options (server.js). It protects users' browsers from other sites; it's not authentication, which is why the endpoints also require a token.

Q10.What is a JWT and how does QUIZZY use it?

A signed token with a payload, including the user ID and an expiry. Supabase issues it at login; supabase-js stores it and refreshes it. The client sends it as Authorization: Bearer on REST calls (apiFetch) and in the socket handshake (hostSocket). The server verifies it with supabase.auth.getUser and then trusts the user ID for authorization.

Q11.How do you protect pages in React?

RequireAuth wraps the host routes: it shows a spinner while the session loads, redirects to /login with a from path if there is no user, and otherwise renders the page. But that's only user experience: the real protection is server-side in requireAuth and the socket checks, because client code can be modified.

Q12.What does Zod do in your project?

It validates data at the server's edges: quizSchema for saved quizzes, generateRequestSchema for AI requests, and generatedSchema for the AI's output. safeParse gives me cleaned data or the first readable error message, which I return as a 400. It also strips unknown fields, which blocks mass assignment.

Q13.What is vercel.json for?

It rewrites every path to index.html. QUIZZY is a single-page app, so /join/483920 isn't a real file; without the rewrite, scanning the QR code would give a Vercel 404. With it, React Router reads the path and shows PlayerPage.

Q14.Why are quizzes in the database but games in memory?

Quizzes must survive forever and are read rarely; games are short-lived, change on every answer, and need instant updates. So I load the quiz once when the room is created, run the whole game in the rooms Map, and write the results once at the end. That's two database operations per game instead of one per answer. The trade-off is that a restart loses running games.

Q15.How is the score calculated?

On the server, in room.service → submitAnswer: 10 points (POINTS_PER_CORRECT) for a correct answer, nothing for a wrong one, no time bonus. The client only sends which option it chose; it never sends whether it was right or its score.

Q16.Why Tailwind CSS?

Utility classes let me style quickly and consistently, and Tailwind v4's @theme turns my design tokens (answer colors, fonts, card shadow) into classes like bg-answer-red. Responsive prefixes made it easy to build phone-first student screens and projector-sized host screens, and motion-reduce: lets me respect reduced-motion settings.

Q17.What does express.json() do?

It's middleware that parses a JSON request body into req.body. It also rejects invalid JSON with a 400 and bodies larger than 100 kB by default, which is a cheap first line of defence before Zod validation.

Q18.What is the difference between the host and the student in the system?

Hosts have Supabase accounts and are identified by their verified user ID; they own quizzes (creator_id) and rooms (hostId). Students are anonymous, identified only by their socket.id for one connection. That asymmetry is deliberate (no sign-up friction in class), and it explains why hosts can resume after a refresh but students can't yet.

13.2 Intermediate

Q19.Walk me through what happens when a student taps an answer.

handleAnswer ignores the tap if a result is already shown or a request is in flight, marks the tile and emits quiz:answer with the room code, question index and option index. submitAnswer checks the room is playing, the sender is a player, the index matches their current question and the option is a valid integer; then it scores and advances currentQuestionIndex. The student gets quiz:answer:result with correct, correctOption, score and the next public question; the host gets leaderboard:update. "Next" just displays nextQuestion locally.

Q20.How do you stop students from cheating?

Four layers. The answer key never leaves the server before a student answers (getPublicQuestion only sends text and options). Scoring happens only on the server. questionIndex must equal the player's current index, so you can't answer twice or replay a correct answer. And options are range-checked. What I can't stop is two students sharing a phone screen; that is outside software.

Q21.Explain socket.emit, io.to(id) and io.to(room) with QUIZZY examples.

socket.emit replies only to the sender, e.g. quiz:answer:result or player:join:error. io.to(player.id) targets one other socket through its automatic personal room, e.g. sending each player their first quiz:question when the host starts. io.to(code) reaches everyone in the game, e.g. room:players and room:closed. io.to("host:"+code) reaches only host screens, for leaderboard:update.

Q22.Why a separate host:CODE room?

The leaderboard contains everyone's scores and is sent on every answer. Sending it to CODE would push the whole class's data to every phone on every answer: wasted bandwidth and information students don't need. A host-only room also lets several host tabs stay in sync, and the disconnect handler uses its size to decide whether the host is truly gone.

Q23.How are sockets authenticated?

The host socket's auth option is an async function that reads the current session and returns { token }; Socket.IO calls it on every connection and reconnection, so it's always fresh. On the server, io.use(socketAuth) verifies it with supabase.auth.getUser and stores the user ID in socket.data.userId, which the client can't modify. Host-only handlers check that value.

Q24.Why doesn't socketAuth reject connections without a token?

Because students are supposed to connect anonymously through the same Socket.IO server. The middleware only labels the connection; authorization happens per event: host:create-room requires a user ID, and startQuiz/endQuiz compare it with room.hostId. An invalid token simply becomes an anonymous socket, which can do nothing a student can't.

Q25.Why return 404 instead of 403 for someone else's quiz?

A 403 confirms the quiz exists, which helps an attacker enumerate valid IDs. Returning the same 404 for "doesn't exist" and "not yours" reveals nothing. getQuiz does this, and the socket handler uses the same "Quiz not found" message. GitHub does the same for private repos.

Q26.Why did you use a Postgres function to save a quiz?

Saving writes one row to quizzes and many rows to questions, and it must be all-or-nothing. supabase-js can't run a transaction across several calls, but a Postgres function call is a single statement and therefore atomic. So create_quiz does both inserts and returns the ID, in one round trip. The same pattern is used for save_session_results.

Q27.How do you make the AI output reliable?

Four steps in ai.service.js. A strict prompt (exactly 4 options, one correct, vary the position). Structured output with a JSON schema, so Gemini must return { questions: [...] }. Then JSON.parse plus Zod validation with the same questionSchema human quizzes use, with a second attempt if it fails. Finally, nothing is saved automatically: the host reviews and edits before saving.

Q28.What happens if Gemini is down or overloaded?

callWithRetry retries transient errors (HTTP 429, 500, 503) twice with exponential backoff (1 s, then 2 s). Other errors fail immediately. If everything fails, the controller logs the details and returns a generic 502 "Could not generate questions. Please try again.", and the page shows it in the AI card. Worst case is 2 attempts × 3 calls = 6 Gemini calls for one click, which is why rate limiting matters.

Q29.How are leaderboard ranks computed, including ties?

getLeaderboard sorts by score descending, with nickname as a tie-breaker for a stable order. Each player's rank is the index of the first player with the same score, plus one. So scores 30, 20, 20, 10 give ranks 1, 2, 2, 4: standard "competition ranking". The same ranks are sent to students in quiz:ended and saved to the database.

Q30.How does the host page survive a refresh?

Hosts are identified by user ID, not socket ID. On every connect, HostPage emits host:resume; the server finds the host's room with findRoomByHost, cancels the pending close timer, re-joins the socket to CODE and host:CODE, and sends room:resumed plus the current leaderboard. The UI rebuilds itself from that, and the game never stopped for students.

Q31.Explain the 60-second grace period.

When the last host socket of a room disconnects, the server doesn't close the room immediately: it starts a setTimeout stored in room.closeTimer. If the host resumes, the timer is cleared. If not, the callback first checks getRoom(room.code) === room (the room might have been closed and the code reused), then sends room:closed to students and deletes the room. Without the grace period, a teacher's accidental refresh would kick out the whole class.

Q32.What happens when a student's phone disconnects?

removePlayer removes them entirely if the game is still in the lobby (and re-broadcasts the list); during the game it keeps their score but sets connected: false, and the host's board fades their row with "(disconnected)". They currently can't come back, because their new socket has a new ID and joins are closed once playing.

Q33.What is the difference between the Supabase publishable and secret keys?

The publishable key is public (it's in the JavaScript bundle) and acts as an anonymous or logged-in user, restricted by Row Level Security; I only use it for Auth in the browser. The secret key bypasses RLS and gives full database access; it lives only in Render's environment and server/.env, used by db/supaBase.js. Putting the secret key in a VITE_ variable would publish it.

Q34.Why are there two socket modules on the client?

socket/socket.js is the anonymous student socket used by PlayerPage; hostSocket.js sends the JWT in its handshake and is used by HostPage. Separating them keeps student connections token-free, gives each page exactly one connection with its own listeners, and makes it possible to test host and student in two tabs of one browser.

Q35.Node is single-threaded. Can two events still conflict?

Synchronous code can't interleave, so submitAnswer never runs twice at the same instant. But an await lets other events run in between. In host:create-room I await the database; meanwhile a double click could start a second creation. So I set socket.data.creatingRoom before awaiting, and after the await I re-check socket.connected and findRoomByHost before creating the room.

Q36.Why identify students by socket.id, and what does that cost?

It needs zero setup: no account, no stored ID, and the server already has it. It also lets me use io.to(player.id) directly. The cost is that identity dies with the connection: a dropped phone becomes a stranger and its score is orphaned. The fix is a random player ID kept in sessionStorage and a rejoin event.

Q37.How do the leaderboard rows slide when ranks change?

Each row is a motion.li with the layout prop and a stable key={player.id}. When the sorted list re-renders, motion measures each row's old and new position, applies a transform that puts it back where it was, then animates the transform to zero: the FLIP technique. MotionConfig reducedMotion="user" turns the movement off for users who prefer reduced motion.

Q38.How does the student's page know the join succeeded?

There's no dedicated "joined" event: handlePlayers sets joined = true when a room:players list arrives, and the server only sends that to sockets in the room, which happens after a successful addPlayer. It works, but it's implicit; an explicit acknowledgement on player:join would be clearer and would let the student's own nickname come from the server.

13.3 Advanced

Q39.How would you scale QUIZZY to many server instances?

Today all state is in one process: the rooms Map and Socket.IO's socket-room membership. To scale out I would move room state into Redis (atomic operations per answer), add the Socket.IO Redis adapter so io.to(code) reaches sockets on any instance, enable sticky sessions on the load balancer (needed for long-polling), and move the rate-limit counters into Redis. Timers like the grace period would become Redis keys with expiry.

Q40.Describe a race condition you handled.

host:create-room awaits getQuizById. During that await, the same host could click again, or open a second tab, or disconnect. I guard with a per-socket creatingRoom flag (cleared in finally), and after the await I re-check that the socket is still connected and that findRoomByHost still finds nothing. Otherwise a host could end up with two rooms, or an orphan room nobody can control.

Q41.What's the weakness of checking the token only at the socket handshake?

A host socket stays authorized for as long as it is connected, even after the JWT expires or the user signs out elsewhere. For a 30-minute class game that's acceptable. For stricter needs I'd re-verify on sensitive events (start, end, close), or schedule a disconnect at the token's exp so the client reconnects with a fresh token.

Q42.getUser(token) vs verifying the JWT locally: which and why?

getUser asks Supabase on every request: simple, and it catches revoked sessions or deleted users, but it adds latency and depends on Supabase being reachable (hence the 500 "Could not verify session" path). Local verification with the project's public signing keys is fast and works offline, but a token stays valid until it expires. At higher traffic I'd verify locally and keep tokens short-lived.

Q43.There's a bug in the AI rate limiting. Explain it and the fix.

quiz.routes.js registers POST /generate twice: first router.post("/generate", quizController.generateQuiz), then the version with aiRateLimit. Express runs the first match; generateQuiz sends a response and never calls next(), so the second registration and the limiter never run. The fix is to delete the first line. I'd also add a test that the eleventh request in an hour gets a 429.

Q44.How would you let students reconnect?

Generate a random playerId on the client (crypto.randomUUID()), store it in sessionStorage, and send it with player:join. The server keys players by playerId and stores the current socketId separately. On reconnect, a player:rejoin { roomCode, playerId } event updates the socket ID, joins the socket room, sets connected: true and re-sends the player's current question. Personal messages would then use io.to(player.socketId).

Q45.Can a malicious client crash the server?

Yes, and I verified it. The quiz:start handler destructures ({ roomCode }) without a default, so emitting quiz:start with no payload throws a TypeError that nothing catches, and the Node process exits, ending every game. Any anonymous socket can send it. host:close-room calls ack() without checking that it is a function. I'd validate every socket payload with Zod (like the REST side), give every handler a default parameter, and wrap handlers in a helper that catches and logs errors so one bad message can never affect other games.

Q46.What about prompt injection through the topic field?

The topic is inserted into the prompt, so a host could write "ignore the rules and…". The impact is limited: only logged-in hosts can call it, the topic is capped at 100 characters, the response must match a JSON schema and pass Zod, and the host reviews everything before saving. The worst case is odd questions in the host's own quiz. I'd still keep the topic clearly delimited in the prompt and could add content moderation for a school product.

Q47.How would you make running games survive a server restart?

Store room snapshots outside the process, ideally in Redis, updated on every change, with a TTL. On startup or on host:resume, load the room back. Socket connections would still drop during a deploy, but both hosts (by user ID) and students (with the stable playerId from Q44) could resume. Also, deploys should avoid class times, and a paid instance avoids free-tier sleep.

Q48.How would you add a time limit per question fairly?

The server must own time. When it sends a question to a player, store questionSentAt on the player; in submitAnswer, reject or score zero if Date.now() - questionSentAt exceeds the limit (plus a small network allowance). The client countdown is only a display. Speed bonuses would be computed the same way, never from a client timestamp.

Q49.Are there memory leaks?

Slow ones. A finished room stays in the Map until the host closes it or disconnects for 60 s; a host who leaves the results open for days keeps it alive. The rate-limit Map keeps an entry for every user who ever generated (old timestamps are filtered but the key stays). Fixes: a periodic sweep that deletes rooms finished more than N minutes ago or idle too long, and deleting empty rate-limit entries (or a TTL store).

Q50.Your server bypasses RLS with the secret key. Why bother with RLS?

Defence in depth. The publishable key is public, so if RLS were off, anyone could query Supabase's REST API directly and download every quiz including answers, bypassing my server entirely. With RLS enabled and no policies, that key can't touch the tables, and my server, which does its own ownership checks, is the only door.

Q51.How would you test this?

room.service.js and question.service.js are mostly pure functions over plain objects, so I'd unit-test them first: joining rules, duplicate nicknames, answer order, scoring, tie ranks. Then integration tests that start the HTTP + Socket.IO server on a random port and drive two socket.io-client instances through a full game. REST controllers can be tested with supertest and a mocked Supabase client. Finally, a GitHub Actions workflow running lint and tests before deploys.

Q52.What if saving the results fails at the end of a game?

Today the error is logged and the host gets a host:error, but the results are lost once the room is closed. Because save_session_results is one transaction, there's never a half-saved session. To make it reliable I'd retry with backoff, and keep the payload until it succeeds (or write it to a local queue, the "outbox" pattern), and only allow closing the room after a successful save or explicit confirmation.

Q53.How does QUIZZY handle a host with two tabs open?

Both tabs resume the same room via host:resume and join host:CODE, so both get leaderboard updates. On disconnect, the server counts the remaining sockets in host:CODE and only starts the close timer when the count is zero, so closing one tab doesn't threaten the game. A second tab's host:create-room is refused by findRoomByHost.

Q54.Why is quiz:question only sent once?

Only the first question is pushed, at start. Every following question rides along in quiz:answer:result.nextQuestion, because the server advances the player at the moment of answering. That saves a round trip per question and keeps the server as the single source of truth for each player's position; the "Next" button is purely a UI pause to read the feedback.

13.4 Behavioral

These answers must be honest and in your own words. The notes below point to real material in this codebase you can build them from.

Q55.What was the hardest bug you faced?

Pick a real one and use the STAR shape (Situation, Task, Action, Result). This codebase contains good candidates: the production deployment (commits "deployement chnages" and "chore: trigger Vercel deploy"), where things that work locally break because of CLIENT_URL/CORS, a missing VITE_API_URL falling back to localhost, or a VITE_ change that needs a rebuild; or the host refresh problem that led to identifying hosts by user ID plus host:resume and the grace timer. Explain how you found the cause (browser console, Network tab, Render logs, the debug console.logs still in socketAuth.js and quiz.routes.js) and what you changed so it can't recur.

Q56.Which decision would you change?

A strong, honest answer: "Identifying students by socket.id. It was the quickest path, but it means a phone that drops Wi-Fi loses the game. I'd give each player a stable random ID from the start." Alternatives: creating the schema in the dashboard instead of committed migrations, or not validating socket payloads with Zod the way REST bodies are. Always add what you'd do instead and why you didn't at first (speed of the first version).

Q57.What did you learn from this project?

Good themes with evidence: the difference between authentication and authorization (Supabase vs your ownership checks); never trusting the client, or the AI; how deployment shapes architecture (why the server is on Render); and the cost of in-memory state. Close with one concrete next step, like adding tests for room.service.

Q58.If you had two more weeks, what would you build?

Prioritize and justify: (1) fix the rate-limit route and validate socket payloads, because they're security issues; (2) student reconnection, because it's the biggest real-classroom problem; (3) a "past sessions" page, since results are already saved but never shown; (4) tests and CI. Prioritizing by risk and user impact is itself the signal interviewers look for.

14.Issues found while reading the code

These were found while writing this guide. None of them have been fixed; the code was not modified. Severity: High security or availability risk, Medium a real bug users can hit, Low clean-up, inconsistency or dead code.

14.1 Bugs and risks

1. One malformed socket message crashes the whole server High

server/src/sockets/socket.js, handler quiz:start: socket.on("quiz:start", ({ roomCode }) => …) destructures its argument with no default. Emitting quiz:start with no payload throws a TypeError inside the handler. Verified with a minimal reproduction using the project's own socket.io version: the error is not caught, and the Node process exits. Any anonymous student socket can do this, and it ends every running game on the server. The other handlers use (data = {}), which only helps for undefined; a null payload would throw the same way. host:close-room calls ack() without checking it is a function.

Suggested fix: validate every socket payload with Zod (as REST bodies are), and wrap handlers in a helper that catches and logs errors.

2. The AI rate limiter never runs High

server/src/routes/quiz.routes.js lines 13–14 register POST /generate twice; the first registration has no aiRateLimit. Express stops at the first matching handler, which sends the response, so the limiter is unreachable and AI generation is unlimited (up to 6 Gemini calls per request with retries).

Suggested fix: delete line 13.

3. Quiz ownership depends on Zod stripping fields Medium

quiz.controller.js → createQuiz calls createQuiz({ creatorId: req.user.id, ...result.data }). Because the spread comes last, a creatorId inside result.data would override the real one. It is safe today only because quizSchema (a plain z.object) drops unknown keys; a future .passthrough() or schema change would silently allow creating quizzes as another user.

Suggested fix: put creatorId: req.user.id after the spread.

4. room:players sends too much to every student Medium

socket.js emits the raw room.players array (socket IDs, scores, progress, connection state) to the whole room on every join and lobby disconnect. Students only need nicknames. It is the one place that does not use a field allowlist like getLeaderboard.

5. Resume ignores which quiz was opened Medium

host:resume uses findRoomByHost(userId) and ignores the :quizId in the URL. If quiz A has a room and the host opens /host/<quiz B>, the page resumes quiz A's room. Creating a room for B fails with "You already have a running room" until A's room is closed.

6. Finished rooms and rate-limit entries are never cleaned up Medium

A finished room stays in the rooms Map until the host clicks "Back to my quizzes" or disconnects for 60 s; a host who leaves the results tab open keeps it in memory indefinitely. aiRateLimit.js filters old timestamps but never deletes a user's key. Both grow slowly over a long-running process.

7. Students can't recover from a dropped connection Medium

Players are identified by socket.id, and addPlayer rejects joins after the start. After a Wi-Fi drop, Socket.IO reconnects with a new ID, but PlayerPage never re-joins: the student stays on a question whose answers now fail with "Only players can answer".

8. No feedback when the server is unreachable Medium

PlayerPage's connect_error handler only calls console.error, so Join appears to do nothing. On HostPage, checking only becomes false after a server reply, so the "Checking for a running session..." spinner never ends if the server is asleep or down.

9. Sign-up with email confirmation silently bounces Medium

LoginPage.jsx → handleSubmit navigates after signUp without checking data.session (the data variable is unused). If "Confirm email" is enabled in Supabase, there is no session yet, RequireAuth redirects back to /login, and the user is never told to check their email.

10. Results are lost if saving fails Medium

quiz:end calls saveSessionResults once. On failure the host gets host:error, but there is no retry, and closing the room discards the data.

11. Smaller client-side bugs Low

  • LoginPage ignores loading from useAuth(), so a logged-in host briefly sees the login form before the redirect.
  • Leaderboard.jsx → allFinished counts disconnected players as finished, so "Everyone has finished!" appears if everyone disconnects.
  • CreateQuizPage: an empty "Questions" box sends count: Number("") = 0 (the server rejects it with "Ask for at least 1 question"); Save is not disabled while AI generation runs, so the old questions can be saved just before they are replaced.
  • CreateQuizPage → handleSubmit: if the server answers with non-JSON (e.g. an HTML 413 or 500 page), res.json() throws and the user sees the misleading "Could not reach the server".
  • crypto.randomUUID() (in emptyQuestion) only exists in secure contexts (HTTPS or localhost); opening the create page over plain http:// on a LAN IP during testing crashes it.
  • HostPage reports errors with alert().
  • HomePage's room-code input has a placeholder but no label (accessibility), and doesn't use the shared Input/Card components.

12. Socket token checked only at connection Low

socketAuth runs once per connection; a host socket stays authorized after its JWT expires or the user signs out elsewhere, until it reconnects.

14.2 Inconsistencies

13. DECISIONS.md is out of date Low

  • It describes storing questions in questions.js as hardcoded test data; that file is now empty and quizzes come from Supabase.
  • Decision 4 says HTTP is used "for operations such as creating a room"; rooms are created with the host:create-room socket event, and the HTTP room route is commented out.
  • It stops at decision 5 and doesn't record Supabase, authentication, the Postgres functions, Gemini, the grace period, or hosting.

14. Misleading messages and configuration details Low

  • Startup errors say "Missing … in .env" even on Render, where there is no .env and the fix is in the dashboard.
  • client/src/config/config.js uses ??, so an empty VITE_API_URL becomes "" (requests go to the Vercel site) instead of failing.
  • server/package.json has "main": "index.js" (no such file) and "dev": "npx nodemon …" without nodemon as a dependency.
  • The function that creates a room is named roomService, the same as the module, giving calls like roomService.roomService(...); createRoom would be clearer.
  • api.js and hostSocket.js import with "../src/…" paths that leave and re-enter src; "./…" is the normal form.
  • There is no root README.md; client/README.md is the unmodified Vite template. The database schema (four tables) and the two Postgres functions exist only in the Supabase dashboard, not as SQL in the repository.

14.3 Dead code and leftovers

15. Unused files, functions and imports Low

  • server/src/routes/room.routes.js and server/src/controllers/room.controller.js: entirely commented out; also the commented app.use("/api/rooms", …) and // app.use(cors()); in app.js.
  • server/src/data/questions.js: empty file.
  • quiz.service.js → toPublicQuiz: exported, never used.
  • GET /api/quizzes/:id (getQuiz): never called by the client.
  • client/src/App.css (empty), client/src/assets/hero.png, react.svg, vite.svg (unused), and // window.io = io; in App.jsx.
  • Unused imports reported by ESLint: API_URL in QuizListPage.jsx and CreateQuizPage.jsx; StrictMode in main.jsx (the app is not wrapped in it); data in LoginPage.jsx. ESLint also flags AuthContext.jsx for exporting a hook next to a component (breaks fast refresh for that file).

16. Debug logging left in production Low

  • quiz.routes.js: console.log("controller exports:", …) at startup.
  • socketAuth.js: logs every socket connection with its user ID.
  • socket.js disconnect: console.log("DISCONNECT:", socket.id, socket.data) logs user IDs and room codes on every disconnect.

FileWhy

C. Numbers worth remembering

Room code6 digits, 100000–999999, unique among live rooms
Points per correct answer10
Host grace period60 seconds
Nickname length1–20 characters, unique (case-insensitive)
Quiz limitstitle ≤ 100; 1–50 questions; text ≤ 300; 2–6 options ≤ 100 chars
AI request limitstopic 3–100 chars; 1–15 questions; easy / medium / hard
AI reliability2 attempts × (1 call + 2 retries at 1 s and 2 s)
AI rate limit (intended)10 generations per user per hour
Close-room acknowledgement timeout3 seconds
